# 12-Week Upper-Body Strength Programme
### Client Profile: 29-year-old recreational climber | Right subacromial impingement (4 months physio, cleared for pain-free range, no overhead loading)

---

## Guiding Principles Before You Begin

**Injury considerations first.** Subacromial impingement typically involves compression of the supraspinatus and/or biceps long-head tendon in the subacromial space. The most provocative positions are internal rotation under load, arm elevation above roughly 90°, and any pressing overhead. All programming below respects the physio's clearance: pain-free range only, zero overhead loading throughout all 12 weeks. If she reports any anterior shoulder pain, clicking with discomfort, or night pain at any point, pause the session and refer back to her physiotherapist before continuing.

**Scapular health is the foundation.** Climbers frequently present with overdeveloped pulling musculature (lats, rhomboids) relative to their serratus anterior and lower trapezius. This imbalance is a common driver of impingement. The programme deliberately prioritises scapular upward rotators and depressors, and keeps horizontal pulling volume high relative to pressing volume throughout.

**Progressive overload is gradual.** Because she is returning from an active injury, load increases are capped at roughly 5–10% per week on any given exercise, and deload weeks are built in at weeks 4 and 8.

**Communicate with the physio.** Share this programme with her physiotherapist. The physio may want to adjust specific exercises based on current clinical findings.

---

## Programme Structure Overview

| Phase | Weeks | Focus |
|---|---|---|
| Phase 1 – Foundation & Scapular Control | 1–4 | Motor control, tissue tolerance, movement quality |
| Phase 2 – Hypertrophy & Strength Base | 5–8 | Volume accumulation, bilateral and unilateral loading |
| Phase 3 – Strength & Power Endurance | 9–12 | Heavier loading, climbing-specific pulling patterns |

**Training frequency:** 3 upper-body sessions per week, ideally with at least one rest day between sessions (e.g. Monday / Wednesday / Friday). Lower-body and cardiovascular work can be programmed around these days as the trainer sees fit.

**Session structure:** Warm-up → Scapular activation block → Main work → Accessory work → Cool-down mobility.

---

## Phase 1: Foundation & Scapular Control (Weeks 1–4)

### Phase Goals
Establish pain-free movement patterns, activate inhibited scapular stabilisers, build connective tissue tolerance, and identify her true working range on every exercise. No exercise should produce pain above a 0/10 during or after the session. Mild muscle fatigue is expected and appropriate; any joint discomfort is not.

---

### Week 1

**Session A – Scapular Activation & Horizontal Pull Focus**

*Warm-up (10 minutes)*
Begin with 5 minutes of light rowing machine or arm-bike at low resistance to increase blood flow to the shoulder girdle without loading the joint. Follow with 2 rounds of: 10 scapular wall slides (arms at 90° "goalpost" position, sliding up only to comfortable range — likely 90–100° for this client), 10 prone Y-raises with no weight (lying face down on a bench, arms at roughly 45° from the body, thumbs up, lifting only to hip height), and 10 band pull-aparts at chest height with a light resistance band.

*Main Work*
**A1. Seated Cable Row (neutral grip, elbows close to body)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Use a light load that allows full scapular retraction and depression at the end range. Cue her to think "chest tall, shoulder blades back and down" rather than pulling with the arm. Rest 90 seconds.

**A2. Face Pull (cable at eye height, rope attachment, external rotation emphasis)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. This is arguably the most important exercise in Phase 1. Pull the rope to the sides of the face, finishing with elbows high and hands behind the ears — but only to the range that is completely pain-free. If she cannot reach the full external rotation endpoint without discomfort, shorten the range and note it. Rest 60 seconds.

**A3. Dumbbell Chest-Supported Row (prone on incline bench, neutral grip, elbows at 45°)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. The chest-supported position removes lumbar loading and forces scapular work. Cue a slight pause at the top of each rep. Rest 90 seconds.

*Accessory Work*
**B1. Serratus Anterior Wall Slide** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Standing facing a wall, forearms on the wall, slide arms upward only to 90° (or pain-free limit). The key movement is protracting the scapula at the top — pushing the wall away with the shoulder blade. This directly targets serratus anterior, which is critical for scapular upward rotation and impingement management.

**B2. Pallof Press (cable or band, standing)** — 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Arms stay at chest height throughout. This is anti-rotation core work that also loads the shoulder in a safe, sub-90° position.

**B3. Dumbbell Bicep Curl (seated, neutral/supinated grip)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Light load, full elbow range, no shoulder compensation.

*Cool-down (5–8 minutes)*
Doorway pec stretch at 90° (not above — avoid the provocative range), cross-body posterior capsule stretch (gently pull the right arm across the chest at shoulder height), and 5 minutes of diaphragmatic breathing to down-regulate the nervous system.

---

**Session B – Pressing Tolerance & Posterior Chain**

*Warm-up* — Same as Session A.

*Main Work*
**A1. Dumbbell Floor Press (neutral grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. The floor press is the safest horizontal pressing option for this client. The floor acts as a natural range limiter, preventing the elbows from dropping below the shoulder plane, which is the most provocative position for impingement. Start with a weight she can control perfectly. Rest 90 seconds.

**A2. Cable Chest Fly (low-to-mid cable, arms staying below 90°)** — 3 sets × 15 reps. Set the cables at roughly hip height. She brings the handles together in front of the chest in a hugging arc, keeping arms below shoulder height throughout. This loads the pectorals without shoulder elevation. Rest 60 seconds.

**A3. Single-Arm Dumbbell Row (bench-supported)** — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. Standard single-arm row, elbow driving back and slightly out. Ensure the right shoulder does not hike or internally rotate under load. Rest 90 seconds.

*Accessory Work*
**B1. Band External Rotation (elbow at side, 90° elbow flexion)** — 3 sets × 15 reps each side. This is a physio staple and should feel like a direct continuation of her rehabilitation work. Light band, controlled movement, no compensation at the shoulder girdle.

**B2. Prone Lower Trap Raise (on incline bench, thumbs up, arms at 135° — "Y" position)** — 3 sets × 10 reps with no weight or very light plates (0.5–1 kg). The lower trapezius is a primary scapular upward rotator and is almost always underactive in impingement presentations. Lift only to hip height.

**B3. Tricep Pushdown (cable, rope attachment)** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Elbows stay at the sides, arms stay below 90°.

*Cool-down* — Same as Session A.

---

**Session C – Unilateral Focus & Rotator Cuff Integration**

*Warm-up* — Same as Sessions A and B.

*Main Work*
**A1. Half-Kneeling Single-Arm Cable Row (elbow at 90°, pulling to hip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. The half-kneeling position adds a stability challenge and prevents the torso from rotating to compensate. Pull the handle to the hip rather than the chest to keep the shoulder in a safe arc.

**A2. Incline Dumbbell Press (bench at 30–45°, neutral grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. A low-incline press keeps the shoulder below 90° of elevation while still loading the anterior deltoid and pectorals. Monitor carefully — if she reports any anterior shoulder discomfort, reduce the incline further or replace with a second floor press variation. Rest 90 seconds.

**A3. TRX or Ring Row (body at roughly 45° to the floor)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Bodyweight horizontal row. Cue scapular retraction and depression at the top. As she gets stronger, she can lower her body angle to increase difficulty.

*Accessory Work*
**B1. Side-Lying External Rotation (dumbbell, right side)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. Classic infraspinatus and teres minor exercise. Very light dumbbell (1–2 kg). Elbow bent to 90°, rotate the forearm upward. This is a direct rotator cuff strengthening exercise and should be treated with the same care as her physio exercises.

**B2. Scapular Depression Hold (on parallel bars or dip station, arms straight, no dip)** — 3 sets × 10-second holds. She simply supports her bodyweight on straight arms and actively depresses the scapulae (pushes the shoulders down away from the ears). This is an isometric lower trapezius and serratus exercise that directly mimics the shoulder position used in climbing.

**B3. Hammer Curl** — 2 sets × 15 reps. Neutral grip, controlled tempo.

*Cool-down* — Same as previous sessions.

---

### Week 2

The structure of all three sessions remains identical to Week 1. The adjustments are as follows: increase the load on all main work exercises by approximately 5% where she achieved all reps with good form in Week 1. Add one additional set to the face pull (now 4 sets × 15) and the prone lower trap raise (now 4 sets × 10), as these are the highest-priority corrective exercises. Begin tracking her pain scores (0–10) at the start and end of each session and after each exercise. If any exercise consistently produces even a 1/10 discomfort, modify the range or load before progressing.

---

### Week 3

Increase load by a further 5% on exercises where she is consistently achieving all reps with good form and zero discomfort. Introduce two technique progressions: on the face pull, begin experimenting with a slightly higher elbow position at the finish if she is pain-free doing so; on the TRX row, lower her body angle by 5–10° to increase the load. Add a tempo prescription to the main compound movements: 3 seconds eccentric, 1-second pause, 1 second concentric (written as 3-1-1). This increases time under tension without requiring heavier loads, which is appropriate at this stage.

---

### Week 4 — Deload

Reduce all working sets by 40% of volume (drop from 3–4 sets to 2 sets on all exercises). Maintain the same loads used in Week 3 — this is a volume deload, not an intensity deload. The purpose is to allow connective tissue recovery and consolidate the motor patterns learned in Weeks 1–3. Use this week to reassess her pain-free range on every exercise and document it clearly, as this will inform Phase 2 loading. She should leave every session feeling refreshed rather than fatigued. This is also an ideal week for her to have a check-in with her physiotherapist to report progress.

---

## Phase 2: Hypertrophy & Strength Base (Weeks 5–8)

### Phase Goals
Increase training volume and load systematically. Introduce new movement patterns that build on the scapular control established in Phase 1. Begin loading the horizontal press more seriously. Maintain the 2:1 pull-to-push ratio throughout. She should now be demonstrating consistent scapular control under load and reporting zero pain during sessions.

---

### Week 5

**Session A – Horizontal Pull Strength**

*Warm-up* — 5 minutes arm-bike, then 2 rounds of: 10 band pull-aparts, 10 face pulls (light band), 10 scapular wall slides.

*Main Work*
**A1. Barbell Bent-Over Row (overhand grip, hinge to roughly 45°)** — 4 sets × 8 reps. This is a significant load increase from the cable and dumbbell rows of Phase 1. Ensure she can maintain a neutral spine and that the right shoulder does not elevate or internally rotate under load. **A2. Weighted TRX Row (add a weight vest or hold a plate on the chest)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. Progressing from the bodyweight version in Phase 1. Rest 90 seconds.

*Accessory Work*
**B1. Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row (elbows flared to 45°, targeting mid-traps)** — 3 sets × 12 reps.

**B2. Band Pull-Apart (overhand grip, arms at chest height)** — 3 sets × 20 reps. High-rep, low-load posterior shoulder work.

**B3. Incline Dumbbell Curl (seated, supinated grip)** — 3 sets × 12 reps. The incline position increases the stretch on the biceps long head — monitor for any anterior shoulder discomfort and revert to a standard seated curl if needed.

*Cool-down* — Pec stretch, posterior capsule stretch, thoracic extension over a foam roller (mid-back mobility, not shoulder loading).

*Warm-up* — Same as Session A.

**B1. Prone Lower Trap Raise (now with 1–2 kg plates)** — 4 sets × 10 reps.

**B2. Side-Lying External Rotation (right side, progressed to 2–3 kg)** — 3 sets × 12 reps.

**B3. Tricep Pushdown (straight bar, pronated grip)** — 3 sets × 15 reps.

*Cool-down* — Same as Session A.

---

**Session C – Unilateral Strength & Rotator Cuff Loading**

*Warm-up* — Same as previous sessions.

*Main Work*
**A1. Single-Arm Cable Row (standing, split stance)** — 4 sets × 10 reps each side. Standing rather than seated increases the stability demand. Ensure the right shoulder does not hike or protract under load.

**A2. Half-Kneeling Landmine Press (right arm)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. The half-kneeling position reduces the ability to compensate through the lower back and forces the shoulder to work in isolation. This is particularly important for the right (affected) side. Rest 90 seconds.

**A3. Neutral-Grip Pull-Down (lat pulldown machine, wide neutral grip, pulling to chin level — not behind the neck)** — 3 sets × 10 reps. This is the first vertical pulling movement in the programme. The neutral grip reduces internal rotation stress at the shoulder. Pull only to chin height — do not allow the elbows to travel behind the body at the bottom of the movement, as this can compress the subacromial space. Rest 2 minutes.

*Accessory Work*
**B1. Scapular Depression Hold (progressed — add a 5 kg dumbbell held between the knees)** — 3 sets × 15-second holds.

**B2. Band External Rotation (elbow at side)** — 3 sets × 15 reps each side. Increase band resistance from Phase 1.

**B3. Hammer Curl (alternating, standing)** — 3 sets × 12 reps.

*Cool-down* — Same as previous sessions.

---

### Week 6

Increase load by 5% on all main compound movements where she achieved all reps with good form in Week 5. Add one additional set to the barbell bent-over row (now 5 sets × 8) and the dumbbell bench press (now 5 sets × 8). Introduce a superset pairing for the accessory work to increase training density: pair the prone lower trap raise with the band pull-apart (B1 + B2 as a superset with 30 seconds rest between exercises and 90 seconds rest between rounds). Continue monitoring the landmine press carefully — this is still a relatively new movement pattern.

---

### Week 7

Increase load by a further 5% on main compound movements. Change the rep scheme on the barbell row and dumbbell bench press to 5 sets × 6 reps at a heavier load (approximately 85% of her current 8-rep working weight). This introduces heavier loading while keeping total volume manageable. On the neutral-grip pull-down, increase the load and reduce reps to 4 sets × 8. Introduce a new accessory exercise: **Cable External Rotation at 90° of abduction** — only if her physiotherapist has cleared this range. This loads the infraspinatus in a more functional position for climbing. If not yet cleared, continue with the side-lying version.

---

### Week 8 — Deload

Same protocol as Week 4: reduce volume by 40%, maintain loads from Week 7. Use this week to reassess all pain-free ranges, particularly on the dumbbell bench press and neutral-grip pull-down, as these are the most demanding movements introduced in Phase 2. Document her working loads on all exercises for Phase 3 planning. Recommend another physiotherapy check-in this week.

---

### Phase Goals
Consolidate strength gains, increase loading on key movements, introduce climbing-specific pulling patterns (particularly scapular retraction and depression under load, which mimic the demands of climbing), and prepare her for a return to more demanding climbing training. # Nutrition Plan: Body Recomposition
### Integrated with 12-Week Upper-Body Strength Programme

---

## Important Framing Note for the Trainer

Body recomposition — simultaneously reducing body fat while building or maintaining lean muscle — is entirely achievable for this client. At 29, with an active background in climbing and now a structured resistance programme, she has the physiological conditions that favour recomposition. However, it is slower than pursuing either goal in isolation, and managing expectations honestly from the start will determine long-term adherence. She is also managing an active injury, which means adequate protein and caloric sufficiency are non-negotiable for tissue repair. Aggressive caloric restriction during a rehabilitation phase is counterproductive and should be explicitly avoided.

**Before implementing any nutrition plan, confirm the following with your client:** no history of disordered eating, no current medical conditions affecting nutrition (thyroid disorders, PCOS, coeliac disease, etc.), no medications that interact with dietary changes, and no food allergies or intolerances beyond what she has already disclosed. If any of these flags are present, refer to a registered dietitian before proceeding. As a personal trainer, you are working within your scope of practice by providing general healthy eating guidance — you are not diagnosing, treating, or prescribing for medical conditions.

---

## Step 1: Establishing Her Numbers

### Estimated Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE)

Without knowing her exact height and weight, the following uses a worked example based on a reasonable estimate for a 29-year-old recreational climber: **65 kg, 167 cm**. Adjust all figures proportionally once you have her actual measurements.

**Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) using the Mifflin-St Jeor equation:**
BMR = (10 × 65) + (6.25 × 167) − (5 × 29) − 161
BMR = 650 + 1,043.75 − 145 − 161
**BMR ≈ 1,388 kcal/day**

**Activity multiplier:** She is training 3 days per week with this programme, likely climbing recreationally 1–2 times per week (though this may be reduced during rehabilitation), and has a general daily activity level. A multiplier of **1.55 (moderately active)** is appropriate, though this should be adjusted downward to 1.4 if climbing is currently paused due to the injury.

**TDEE ≈ 1,388 × 1.55 ≈ 2,150 kcal/day**

### Recomposition Caloric Target

For body recomposition, the goal is to eat at a very modest deficit on rest days and at or slightly above maintenance on training days. This approach — sometimes called caloric cycling — provides the anabolic stimulus needed for muscle protein synthesis on training days while creating a small weekly caloric deficit that drives fat loss over time. The weekly net deficit should not exceed 1,500–2,000 kcal (equivalent to roughly 200–280 g of fat loss per week), and given the injury context, erring toward the conservative end is wise.

**Training days:** TDEE + 100–150 kcal → **approximately 2,250–2,300 kcal**
**Rest days:** TDEE − 300–350 kcal → **approximately 1,800–1,850 kcal**

This creates a weekly net deficit of approximately 600–750 kcal across a typical week of 3 training days and 4 rest days, which is modest, sustainable, and injury-appropriate. She should not feel hungry, depleted, or fatigued on this intake. If she does, increase calories toward maintenance and reassess.

---

## Step 2: Macronutrient Targets

### Protein — The Non-Negotiable Priority

Protein is the single most important macronutrient for this client. It drives muscle protein synthesis, supports rotator cuff and connective tissue repair, preserves lean mass during a caloric deficit, and increases satiety. The research on protein requirements for recomposition consistently points toward the higher end of recommendations, particularly for individuals in a deficit and those recovering from injury.

**Target: 2.0–2.2 g per kg of bodyweight per day**
At 65 kg: **130–143 g protein per day**, every day regardless of training or rest day status.

Distribute protein across a minimum of 4 meals or eating occasions per day. Research by Stuart Phillips and colleagues consistently demonstrates that muscle protein synthesis is maximised when protein is distributed evenly rather than concentrated in one or two large meals. Each eating occasion should contain at least 30–40 g of protein to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis, as this appears to be the approximate threshold for activating the mTOR pathway in most adults.

**Pre-training protein:** Consume 30–40 g of protein within 1–2 hours before each training session. This does not need to be a separate meal — it can be part of a regular meal timed appropriately.

**Post-training protein:** Consume 30–40 g of protein within 2 hours after each training session. The "anabolic window" is wider than once believed, but post-exercise protein intake remains important for recovery and adaptation. A whole-food meal is preferable to a supplement where practical.

**Collagen peptides for injury support:** Emerging research (Shaw et al., 2017; Baar, 2019) suggests that consuming 15 g of hydrolysed collagen or gelatin with vitamin C approximately 60 minutes before exercise may enhance collagen synthesis in tendons and ligaments. Given that she is recovering from a subacromial impingement involving tendon tissue, this is a worthwhile addition. It is not a replacement for dietary protein — it is an addition to it. A simple approach is a small glass of orange juice (for vitamin C) with a collagen peptide supplement taken 60 minutes before each training session.

### Carbohydrates — Fuel for Training and Recovery

Carbohydrates are the primary fuel source for resistance training and are essential for replenishing muscle glycogen, supporting thyroid function, and maintaining training performance. Chronically low carbohydrate intake in active women is associated with hormonal disruption, poor recovery, and increased injury risk — all of which are particularly relevant here.

**Target:**
Training days: **3.5–4.0 g per kg → approximately 228–260 g**
Rest days: **2.5–3.0 g per kg → approximately 163–195 g**

Prioritise carbohydrates around training. The largest carbohydrate portions of the day should be the pre-training meal and the post-training meal. On rest days, distribute carbohydrates more evenly across meals and reduce overall quantity, drawing the caloric difference primarily from carbohydrates rather than protein or fat.

**Carbohydrate quality matters.** The majority of carbohydrate intake should come from minimally processed, fibre-rich sources: oats, sweet potato, brown rice, quinoa, wholegrain bread and pasta, legumes, fruit, and vegetables. These sources provide sustained energy, support gut health, and deliver micronutrients that processed carbohydrates do not. Reserve refined carbohydrates (white rice, white bread, sports drinks) for immediately around training sessions when rapid digestion is advantageous.

### Fat — Hormonal Health and Joint Support

Dietary fat is essential for oestrogen production, joint lubrication, fat-soluble vitamin absorption (A, D, E, K), and cell membrane integrity. Active women who under-eat fat frequently experience hormonal disruption, poor skin and joint health, and impaired recovery. Do not allow fat intake to drop below 1.0 g per kg of bodyweight.

**Target:**
Training days: **1.0–1.1 g per kg → approximately 65–72 g**
Rest days: **1.1–1.2 g per kg → approximately 72–78 g**

Fat intake is slightly higher on rest days as a proportion of total calories because carbohydrates are reduced. This is a practical way to maintain satiety and hormonal health on lower-calorie days.

**Prioritise anti-inflammatory fats.** Given the active inflammatory process in her shoulder, the quality of dietary fat is particularly relevant. Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) have well-documented anti-inflammatory effects and may support tendon healing. Aim for at least 2–3 portions of oily fish per week (salmon, mackerel, sardines, trout) or consider a high-quality fish oil supplement providing 2–3 g of combined EPA and DHA per day if dietary intake is insufficient. Prioritise olive oil, avocado, nuts, and seeds as primary fat sources. Minimise trans fats and limit excessive omega-6 vegetable oils (sunflower, corn, soybean oil), which can promote inflammation when consumed in excess relative to omega-3s.

### Summary Macronutrient Table

| | Training Days | Rest Days |
|---|---|---|
| **Calories** | ~2,250–2,300 kcal | ~1,800–1,850 kcal |
| **Protein** | 130–143 g | 130–143 g |
| **Carbohydrates** | 228–260 g | 163–195 g |
| **Fat** | 65–72 g | 72–78 g |

*Adjust all figures once actual height and weight are confirmed. These are starting targets, not permanent prescriptions.*

---

## Step 3: Micronutrients for Injury Recovery and Training

Beyond macronutrients, several micronutrients are specifically relevant to her situation and deserve deliberate attention. These should be obtained from food first, with supplementation used only to address genuine gaps.

### Vitamin D
Vitamin D is essential for calcium absorption, immune function, muscle function, and — critically — tendon and ligament health. Deficiency is extremely common in the UK and northern latitudes, particularly in winter months, and is associated with increased injury risk and impaired healing. A blood test (available through her GP) is the only way to know her status. In the absence of testing, the NHS recommends 10 mcg (400 IU) daily for the general population, but many sports medicine practitioners recommend 1,000–2,000 IU daily for active individuals, particularly during autumn and winter. Dietary sources include oily fish, egg yolks, and fortified foods, but supplementation is almost always necessary to achieve optimal levels in the UK.

**Food sources to prioritise:** Salmon, mackerel, sardines, eggs, fortified dairy or plant milks.
**Supplement consideration:** 1,000–2,000 IU vitamin D3 daily, ideally taken with a meal containing fat for absorption.

### Vitamin C
Vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen synthesis — it is required for the hydroxylation of proline and lysine, the amino acids that form the triple helix structure of collagen. Without adequate vitamin C, collagen synthesis is impaired regardless of protein intake. It is also a potent antioxidant that supports immune function and reduces oxidative stress from training.

**Target:** 200–500 mg per day from food, which is easily achievable with a varied diet.
**Food sources:** Bell peppers (particularly red and yellow), kiwi fruit, strawberries, citrus fruits, broccoli, Brussels sprouts.
**Note:** As mentioned above, 50 mg of vitamin C taken alongside the pre-training collagen supplement (a small glass of orange juice works well) is specifically timed to support tendon collagen synthesis.

### Magnesium
Magnesium is involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions, including muscle contraction and relaxation, protein synthesis, and sleep quality. Active individuals have higher magnesium requirements and are frequently deficient. Poor sleep quality impairs recovery, growth hormone secretion, and injury healing — all of which are directly relevant here.

**Food sources:** Dark leafy greens (spinach, kale), pumpkin seeds, almonds, dark chocolate (70%+), legumes, whole grains.
**Supplement consideration:** 200–400 mg magnesium glycinate or magnesium bisglycinate taken in the evening. Glycinate forms are better absorbed and less likely to cause gastrointestinal discomfort than magnesium oxide.

### Zinc
Zinc is essential for protein synthesis, immune function, and wound healing. It is frequently under-consumed in diets that are low in red meat or shellfish.

**Food sources:** Oysters (the richest source), beef, pumpkin seeds, chickpeas, lentils, cashews.

### Calcium
Important for bone density and muscle function. Particularly relevant for active women, as female athletes are at higher risk of stress fractures and bone density loss if calcium intake is insufficient.

**Target:** 700–1,000 mg per day from food.
**Food sources:** Dairy products, fortified plant milks, tinned sardines and salmon (with bones), tofu set with calcium sulphate, kale, broccoli.

### Iron
Active women are at risk of iron deficiency, which causes fatigue, impaired oxygen delivery to muscles, and poor recovery. This is worth monitoring, particularly if she reports persistent fatigue during the programme.

**Food sources:** Red meat, liver, dark poultry meat, lentils, spinach, fortified cereals. Pair plant-based iron sources with vitamin C to enhance absorption. Avoid consuming iron-rich foods with tea or coffee, as tannins inhibit iron absorption.

## Step 4: Hydration

Hydration is frequently underestimated as a performance and recovery variable. Even mild dehydration (1–2% of bodyweight) measurably impairs strength, power output, and cognitive function. For joint health specifically, synovial fluid — which lubricates the shoulder joint — is water-based, and chronic under-hydration can contribute to joint stiffness and discomfort.

**General target:** 35 ml per kg of bodyweight per day as a baseline. At 65 kg, this is approximately **2.3 litres per day** from all fluid sources (food contributes roughly 20% of daily fluid intake, so actual drinking target is closer to 1.8–2.0 litres).

**Training day additions:** Add 500–750 ml for each training session, consumed before, during, and after the session. A practical approach is to drink 500 ml in the 2 hours before training, sip 200–300 ml during the session, and drink a further 500 ml in the 2 hours after.

**Electrolytes:** On training days, particularly if she sweats heavily, ensure sodium, potassium, and magnesium intake is adequate. This does not require sports drinks — a balanced diet with adequate salt and potassium-rich foods (bananas, potatoes, avocado) is sufficient for most training sessions under 90 minutes.

**Practical hydration cue:** Urine colour is the simplest monitoring tool. Pale straw yellow indicates good hydration. Dark yellow or amber indicates under-hydration. Clear and colourless may indicate over-hydration, which dilutes electrolytes.

## Step 5: Meal Timing and Structure

### Daily Meal Framework

Rather than prescribing rigid meal plans that are unlikely to be followed long-term, the following framework provides a flexible structure that hits the macronutrient targets while fitting around a normal lifestyle.

**Meal 1 — Breakfast (within 1–2 hours of waking)**
Prioritise protein and complex carbohydrates. This meal sets the tone for blood sugar stability throughout the day and contributes significantly to the daily protein target.

*Example training day breakfast:* 3 scrambled eggs with smoked salmon on 2 slices of wholegrain toast, with a side of sliced tomatoes and a glass of orange juice. Approximately 45 g protein, 45 g carbohydrate, 18 g fat.

*Example rest day breakfast:* Greek yoghurt (full-fat, 200 g) with mixed berries, a tablespoon of chia seeds, and a handful of granola. Approximately 20 g protein, 40 g carbohydrate, 12 g fat.

**Meal 2 — Pre-Training Meal or Mid-Morning Meal (2–3 hours before training on training days)**
On training days, this meal should be the largest carbohydrate meal of the day. On rest days, it is a standard balanced meal.

*Example pre-training meal:* Chicken breast (150 g) with a large portion of brown rice (200 g cooked) and roasted vegetables with olive oil. Approximately 45 g protein, 65 g carbohydrate, 12 g fat.

*Example rest day lunch:* Large salad with tinned tuna (150 g), mixed leaves, cucumber, cherry tomatoes, avocado (half), and a lemon-olive oil dressing with a small wholegrain roll. Approximately 38 g protein, 30 g carbohydrate, 18 g fat.

**Pre-Training Supplement (60 minutes before training on training days)**
15 g hydrolysed collagen peptides with a small glass of orange juice (for vitamin C). This is not a meal — it is a targeted supplement timed for tendon collagen synthesis. It contributes approximately 55–60 kcal and 15 g protein (though collagen protein is not a complete protein and does not count toward the muscle protein synthesis target — it is specifically for connective tissue).

**Meal 3 — Post-Training Meal (within 2 hours of training)**
Prioritise protein and moderate carbohydrates. This is the most important meal of the day for muscle protein synthesis and glycogen replenishment.

*Example post-training meal:* Salmon fillet (180 g) with sweet potato (200 g) and steamed broccoli with a drizzle of olive oil. Approximately 42 g protein, 40 g carbohydrate, 16 g fat.

**Meal 4 — Evening Meal**
Balanced meal with protein, vegetables, and moderate carbohydrates. On rest days, reduce the carbohydrate portion and increase vegetables and fat slightly.

*Example training day dinner:* Beef stir-fry (150 g lean beef) with mixed vegetables, noodles (100 g dry weight), soy sauce, ginger, and sesame oil. Approximately 38 g protein, 55 g carbohydrate, 14 g fat.

*Example rest day dinner:* Baked cod (180 g) with roasted Mediterranean vegetables (courgette, aubergine, peppers, cherry tomatoes) in olive oil, with a small portion of quinoa (80 g cooked). Approximately 40 g protein, 25 g carbohydrate, 14 g fat.

**Optional Evening Snack (if protein target not yet met)**
200 g cottage cheese or 200 g Greek yoghurt with a small handful of mixed nuts. Approximately 25–30 g protein, 8–12 g carbohydrate, 8–12 g fat. Casein protein (found in cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt) digests slowly and provides a sustained amino acid release overnight, which supports muscle protein synthesis during sleep.

## Step 6: Phased Nutrition Adjustments Aligned with Training Phases

### Phase 1 (Weeks 1–4) — Tissue Repair Priority

During Phase 1, the emphasis is on establishing the eating pattern, hitting protein targets consistently, and supporting tissue repair. Do not push the caloric deficit aggressively during this phase. If she is struggling with energy levels, fatigue, or sleep quality, bring calories up to maintenance (approximately 2,150 kcal every day) and reassess. The collagen supplement protocol should begin in Week 1. Focus on food quality and consistency rather than precise tracking — building the habit is more important than hitting exact numbers at this stage.

**Key focus:** Protein consistency, anti-inflammatory foods, collagen protocol, hydration habits.

### Phase 2 (Weeks 5–8) — Recomposition in Full Effect

By Week 5, she should have established consistent eating habits and be tolerating the training load well. This is the phase where the training-day / rest-day caloric cycling becomes most important, as training volume and intensity are increasing. Ensure carbohydrate intake on training days is sufficient to support the increased volume — under-fuelling training sessions in Phase 2 will blunt adaptation and increase injury risk. If she is losing weight faster than 0.5 kg per week, increase calories. If she is gaining weight, reduce rest-day carbohydrates by 20–30 g.

**Key focus:** Caloric cycling adherence, pre- and post-training nutrition timing, monitoring body composition changes.

### Phase 3 (Weeks 9–12) — Performance Nutrition

In Phase 3, training intensity is at its highest. This is not the time to increase the caloric deficit. If anything, consider bringing training-day calories up to maintenance or a slight surplus (2,200–2,300 kcal) to support the heavier loading and ensure she is recovering adequately between sessions. The goal in Phase 3 is to maximise strength adaptation while maintaining the body composition progress made in Phases 1 and 2. Aggressive dieting during a strength phase is counterproductive.

**Key focus:** Adequate fuelling for heavy sessions, sleep and recovery nutrition, maintaining protein targets.

## Step 7: Practical Supplement Summary

The following supplements are evidence-based, relevant to her specific situation, and appropriate within a trainer's scope of practice to recommend as general healthy eating guidance. They are listed in order of priority.

**1. Hydrolysed Collagen Peptides (15 g, 60 minutes pre-training with vitamin C)**
Priority: High. Directly relevant to tendon repair and injury recovery. Well-tolerated, low risk.

**2. Vitamin D3 (1,000–2,000 IU daily with a meal containing fat)**
Priority: High. Deficiency is extremely common and directly relevant to musculoskeletal health. Recommend she gets a blood test to confirm status.

**3. Omega-3 Fish Oil (2–3 g EPA+DHA combined per day)**
Priority: High if oily fish intake is less than 2–3 portions per week. Anti-inflammatory, supports joint and tendon health.

**4. Magnesium Glycinate (200–400 mg in the evening)**
Priority: Moderate-high. Supports sleep quality, muscle recovery, and reduces cramping. Very well tolerated.

**5. Creatine Monohydrate (3–5 g daily, any time)**
Priority: Moderate. Creatine is the most extensively researched performance supplement in existence and has a strong safety profile. It supports strength and power output, increases intramuscular phosphocreatine stores, and has emerging evidence for supporting connective tissue health. It causes a small increase in intramuscular water retention (1–2 kg), which some clients find undesirable in a recomposition context — discuss this with her. If she is comfortable with it, 3–5 g daily is appropriate. No loading phase is necessary.

**6. Whey or Plant Protein Powder**
Priority: Low — food first. Protein powder is a convenient tool for hitting protein targets on busy days, not a necessity. If she struggles to reach 130–143 g of protein from whole foods, a single serving of whey isolate or a high-quality plant protein blend (pea + rice) can bridge the gap. It should not replace more than one whole-food protein source per day.

## Step 8: Monitoring and Adjustment Protocol

Body recomposition progress is notoriously difficult to track with the scale alone, because muscle gain and fat loss can occur simultaneously, leaving bodyweight relatively unchanged while body composition improves significantly. Use multiple tracking methods.

**Bodyweight:** Weigh first thing in the morning, after using the bathroom, before eating or drinking, on the same days each week (e.g. Monday, Wednesday, Friday). Take a weekly average rather than reacting to daily fluctuations. Expect the weekly average to remain relatively stable or decrease very slowly (0–0.3 kg per week) during recomposition.

**Circumference measurements:** Measure waist (at the navel), hips (at the widest point), and upper arm (right and left, at the midpoint of the bicep) every 2 weeks. Waist reduction with stable or increasing arm circumference is a strong indicator of successful recomposition.

**Progress photos:** Every 4 weeks, same lighting, same time of day, same clothing. Changes in body composition are often visible in photos before they are apparent in measurements.

**Performance metrics:** Track strength on key exercises (bent-over row, dumbbell bench press, pull-down). Increasing strength while bodyweight remains stable is a reliable indicator of muscle gain and fat loss occurring simultaneously.

**Energy and recovery:** Ask her to rate her energy levels (1–10) and sleep quality (1–10) at each session check-in. Declining scores over consecutive weeks indicate under-fuelling and should prompt a caloric increase before any other intervention.

**Review points:** Conduct a formal nutrition review at the end of each phase (Weeks 4, 8, and 12) and adjust targets based on the data collected. Recomposition is a dynamic process — the targets set at Week 1 will likely need adjustment by Week 8 as her body composition, training load, and metabolic rate change.

# Cardio Programming: 2x/Week
### Integrated with 12-Week Strength & Nutrition Plan | Goal: Return to Long Climbing Days

---

## Framing the Cardio Goal

Long climbing days are a specific and demanding physiological challenge that most gym-based cardio programmes fail to prepare people for adequately. A full day at the crag or indoor wall typically involves 6–10 hours of intermittent high-intensity effort (individual climbs lasting 2–15 minutes), sustained low-intensity activity (walking approaches, belaying, rest periods), repeated grip and forearm loading, and significant time on the feet on uneven terrain. The cardiovascular demand is not purely aerobic — it sits predominantly in the aerobic-threshold zone with repeated spikes into higher intensities on harder moves, which is sometimes described as oxidative glycolytic or zone 3–4 work in modern training terminology.

The cardio programme therefore has two distinct but complementary objectives. The first is building a broad aerobic base — the engine that allows her to recover quickly between climbs, sustain energy across a full day, and avoid the accumulated fatigue that leads to poor movement and increased injury risk late in a climbing day. The second is developing work capacity at threshold — the ability to sustain moderate-to-hard effort for extended periods without accumulating excessive fatigue, which directly mirrors the demands of a sustained climbing pitch or a long boulder problem session.

Critically, both cardio sessions each week must be completely shoulder-friendly. No rowing machine (which loads the shoulder in a pulling pattern that may be provocative under fatigue), no swimming (overhead and rotational shoulder loading), and no exercises that require the arms to be elevated or loaded above 90°. The lower body and cardiovascular system can be trained intensely and effectively without touching the shoulder at all.

---

## Cardio Session Placement Within the Weekly Schedule

The strength programme runs Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The two cardio sessions should be placed on two of the remaining days — Tuesday and Thursday is the recommended placement, as this distributes training stress evenly across the week and ensures she never has more than two consecutive training days. Saturday and Sunday become full rest and recovery days, which is appropriate given the total training volume.

**Recommended weekly schedule:**

| Day | Session |
|---|---|
| Monday | Upper-body strength (Session A) |
| Tuesday | Cardio Session 1 |
| Wednesday | Upper-body strength (Session B) |
| Thursday | Cardio Session 2 |
| Friday | Upper-body strength (Session C) |
| Saturday | Active recovery or complete rest |
| Sunday | Complete rest |

If her climbing sessions resume during the programme — which is the goal — they should replace one of the Saturday or Sunday rest days initially, and later one of the cardio sessions in Phase 3 as her shoulder tolerates it. Discuss this with her physiotherapist before she returns to climbing.

---

## Equipment and Modality Selection

All cardio modalities are selected for zero or minimal shoulder involvement. The following are appropriate and available in a full gym setting.

**Treadmill (walking and running):** The most directly transferable modality to climbing days, which almost always involve significant walking — often on steep, uneven terrain with a heavy pack. Incline treadmill walking in particular is an excellent proxy for approach hiking and builds the hip flexors, glutes, and calves in a pattern directly relevant to mountain and crag environments.

**Stationary Bike (upright or recumbent):** Excellent aerobic base builder with zero shoulder involvement. The recumbent bike is particularly appropriate in Phase 1 when overall fatigue management is a priority. The upright bike more closely mimics the forward-lean posture of approach hiking.

**Ski Erg:** Use with caution and only from Phase 2 onward. The ski erg involves a pulling motion with the arms, but the arms stay below 90° throughout the movement and the shoulder is not loaded in an impingement-provocative position. It is an outstanding full-body aerobic tool and has reasonable climbing specificity (the pulling pattern and core engagement are relevant). Introduce it carefully, monitor for any shoulder discomfort, and abandon it immediately if she reports any pain. Do not use in Phase 1.

**Stair Climber / StepMill:** Highly specific to climbing days. The stair climber directly trains the hip extensors, quadriceps, and calves in a stepping pattern that closely mimics approach hiking and scrambling. It also builds the postural endurance of the trunk and lower back, which is relevant for sustained climbing days. This is arguably the highest-priority cardio modality for her goal.

**Assault Bike (fan bike):** The assault bike involves arm pushing and pulling, which makes it potentially provocative for the shoulder, particularly at high intensities when form breaks down. Avoid in Phases 1 and 2. It may be introduced very cautiously in Phase 3 at low intensity only, with arms kept relaxed and driving primarily with the legs — but the stair climber and treadmill are preferable and lower risk.

**Elliptical:** The elliptical involves arm movement but at low load and below 90° of elevation. It is acceptable as a warm-up tool or low-intensity option but is not the primary modality for this programme due to its low specificity to climbing demands.

---

## Training Zones

The programme uses a simple three-zone model based on perceived exertion (RPE on a 1–10 scale) and approximate heart rate ranges, as heart rate monitors are not always available and RPE is a reliable self-regulation tool once clients understand it.

**Zone 1 — Easy / Aerobic Recovery**
RPE 3–4 out of 10. Conversational pace — she can speak in full sentences without effort. Heart rate approximately 50–65% of maximum. This zone builds aerobic base, enhances fat oxidation, promotes active recovery, and develops the mitochondrial density that underpins all higher-intensity work. It corresponds to the sustained low-intensity activity of a climbing day — the walk-in, belaying, resting between routes.

**Zone 2 — Aerobic Threshold / Steady State**
RPE 5–6 out of 10. She can speak in short sentences but would not choose to hold a long conversation. Heart rate approximately 65–80% of maximum. This is the primary training zone for aerobic base development and is the zone most associated with mitochondrial biogenesis and cardiovascular adaptation. It corresponds to a sustained moderate hiking pace or the aerobic demand of climbing moderate routes continuously.

**Zone 3 — Threshold / Hard Effort**
RPE 7–8 out of 10. Speaking is difficult — short phrases only. Heart rate approximately 80–90% of maximum. This zone develops lactate threshold and the ability to sustain hard efforts, which corresponds to the demands of a sustained hard climbing pitch or a long boulder problem session. Used sparingly and only in structured intervals.

**Zone 4 — High Intensity (used only in specific intervals)**
RPE 9–10 out of 10. Cannot speak. Heart rate above 90% of maximum. Used only in short sprint intervals in Phase 3. Develops peak power output and the ability to recover quickly from maximal efforts — relevant to hard moves on a route.

## Phase 1: Cardio Programming (Weeks 1–4)
### Build the Aerobic Foundation

**Phase 1 Objective:** Establish consistent aerobic training habits, build base aerobic capacity, and prepare the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal systems for higher-intensity work in Phases 2 and 3. All work in Phase 1 is Zone 1–2. No intervals, no high intensity. The body is already adapting to a new strength programme and managing an active injury — adding high-intensity cardio on top of this in Week 1 is a recipe for overreaching.

---

### Cardio Session 1 (Tuesday) — Steady-State Aerobic Base
**Modality:** Stair climber or incline treadmill walk
**Primary zone:** Zone 1–2

**Week 1:**
Begin with 25 minutes total. Spend the first 5 minutes at a very easy pace (Zone 1, RPE 3) as a cardiovascular warm-up. Progress to a moderate pace (Zone 2, RPE 5–6) for 15 minutes. Return to Zone 1 for the final 5 minutes as a cool-down. On the stair climber, use a step rate that allows her to maintain an upright posture without gripping the handles — holding the handles reduces the postural and lower-body demand significantly and should be discouraged except for brief balance checks. On the incline treadmill, set the incline to 8–10% and walk at a pace that achieves Zone 2 without running.

**Week 2:**
Increase total duration to 30 minutes. Maintain the same structure: 5 minutes Zone 1, 20 minutes Zone 2, 5 minutes Zone 1. Increase the stair climber step rate or treadmill incline slightly if Week 1 felt easy.

**Week 3:**
Increase total duration to 35 minutes. 5 minutes Zone 1, 25 minutes Zone 2, 5 minutes Zone 1. Begin introducing brief incline variations on the treadmill if using that modality — alternate between 8% and 12% incline every 5 minutes to simulate the varied terrain of an approach hike.

**Week 4 (Deload):**
Reduce duration to 20 minutes. 5 minutes Zone 1, 10 minutes Zone 2, 5 minutes Zone 1. This mirrors the deload in the strength programme. Keep the effort easy and restorative.

---

### Cardio Session 2 (Thursday) — Aerobic Variety and Duration
**Modality:** Stationary bike (upright) or combination of bike and stair climber
**Primary zone:** Zone 1–2

**Week 1:**
30 minutes on the stationary bike at Zone 2 (RPE 5–6). The bike is lower impact than the stair climber and provides active recovery for the legs while still building aerobic capacity. Maintain a cadence of 80–90 RPM at a resistance that achieves Zone 2 without requiring a cadence below 70 RPM (grinding a high resistance at low cadence is hard on the knees and does not develop aerobic capacity efficiently).

**Week 2:**
35 minutes. Same structure. Increase resistance slightly if Week 1 felt easy at Zone 2.

**Week 3:**
40 minutes. Introduce a simple fartlek element in the final 10 minutes: every 2 minutes, increase resistance or pace to RPE 6–7 for 30 seconds, then return to Zone 2. This is not formal interval training — it is a gentle introduction to effort variation that prepares the body for the structured intervals in Phase 2.

**Week 4 (Deload):**
25 minutes at Zone 1–2. Easy and restorative.

---

## Phase 2: Cardio Programming (Weeks 5–8)
### Aerobic Development and Threshold Introduction

**Phase 2 Objective:** Increase aerobic volume, introduce structured threshold intervals, and begin developing the work capacity that underpins long climbing days. By the end of Phase 2, she should be able to sustain 45–50 minutes of continuous Zone 2 effort and complete structured intervals at Zone 3 without excessive fatigue.

---

### Cardio Session 1 (Tuesday) — Threshold Interval Development
**Modality:** Stair climber (primary) or incline treadmill
**Primary zone:** Zone 2 with Zone 3 intervals

**Week 5:**
Total session: 35 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up, then 4 rounds of (4 minutes Zone 2 + 2 minutes Zone 3), then 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down. The Zone 3 efforts should feel genuinely hard — RPE 7–8 — but not maximal. On the stair climber, increase the step rate significantly for the Zone 3 intervals. On the treadmill, increase the incline to 14–15% or add a slight jog. Rest between intervals is active (Zone 2), not passive — she keeps moving throughout.

**Week 6:**
Total session: 38 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1, then 5 rounds of (4 minutes Zone 2 + 2 minutes Zone 3), then 5 minutes Zone 1. One additional interval round compared to Week 5.

**Week 7:**
Total session: 40 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1, then 5 rounds of (5 minutes Zone 2 + 2 minutes Zone 3), then 5 minutes Zone 1. The Zone 2 portions are longer, increasing the total threshold stimulus.

**Week 8 (Deload):**
Total session: 25 minutes. Return to pure Zone 2 — no intervals. 5 minutes Zone 1, 15 minutes Zone 2, 5 minutes Zone 1.

---

### Cardio Session 2 (Thursday) — Long Aerobic Endurance
**Modality:** Combination session — stair climber + incline treadmill walk, or extended bike session
**Primary zone:** Zone 2 (sustained)

This session is the most directly relevant to the goal of long climbing days. It trains the aerobic system's ability to sustain effort over an extended period, builds fat oxidation capacity, and develops the postural and lower-body muscular endurance needed for a full day on the hill or at the crag. The key word is sustained — she should maintain Zone 2 throughout without drifting into Zone 3, which would compromise the aerobic adaptation and increase fatigue.

**Week 5:**
40 minutes continuous Zone 2. If using a combination approach, spend 20 minutes on the stair climber and 20 minutes on the incline treadmill. The transition between modalities is a useful mental break and also shifts the muscular demand slightly, which is more specific to the varied demands of a climbing day.

**Week 6:**
45 minutes continuous Zone 2. Same combination approach if desired. Increase the stair climber portion to 25 minutes and the treadmill to 20 minutes.

**Week 7:**
50 minutes continuous Zone 2. This is a meaningful aerobic session — the equivalent of a moderate approach hike. Ensure she is fuelling appropriately for this session (see nutrition integration notes below). 25 minutes stair climber, 25 minutes incline treadmill.

**Week 8 (Deload):**
30 minutes continuous Zone 1–2. Easy and restorative.

---

## Phase 3: Cardio Programming (Weeks 9–12)
### Work Capacity, Climbing Specificity, and Peak Preparation

**Phase 3 Objective:** Develop the specific work capacity needed for long climbing days — the ability to sustain repeated moderate-to-hard efforts across many hours with adequate recovery between efforts. Introduce higher-intensity intervals that mimic the cardiovascular demands of hard climbing. By the end of Week 12, she should have the aerobic and threshold fitness to comfortably manage a full climbing day without excessive fatigue.

---

### Cardio Session 1 (Tuesday) — High-Intensity Interval Development
**Modality:** Stair climber or incline treadmill
**Primary zone:** Zone 2–3 with Zone 4 spikes

**Week 9:**
Total session: 40 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1 warm-up, then 6 rounds of (3 minutes Zone 2 + 90 seconds Zone 3 + 30 seconds Zone 4), then 5 minutes Zone 1 cool-down. The Zone 4 efforts are short and maximal — she should be working as hard as she can for 30 seconds. On the stair climber, this means maximum step rate. On the treadmill, maximum incline and pace. The 3-minute Zone 2 recovery between rounds is active and should feel genuinely restorative before the next hard effort. This structure mimics the cardiovascular pattern of climbing — sustained moderate effort punctuated by brief maximal efforts on hard moves.

**Week 10:**
Total session: 42 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1, then 7 rounds of (3 minutes Zone 2 + 90 seconds Zone 3 + 30 seconds Zone 4), then 5 minutes Zone 1. One additional round.

**Week 11:**
Total session: 45 minutes.
Structure: 5 minutes Zone 1, then 8 rounds of (3 minutes Zone 2 + 90 seconds Zone 3 + 30 seconds Zone 4), then 5 minutes Zone 1. This is the peak interval session of the programme. It is demanding — ensure she is well-fuelled and well-rested going into this session.

**Week 12 — Final Week:**
Total session: 30 minutes. Return to Zone 2 only. This is a taper week — reduce intensity and volume to allow full recovery and consolidation of adaptations before she returns to climbing. 5 minutes Zone 1, 20 minutes Zone 2, 5 minutes Zone 1.

---

### Cardio Session 2 (Thursday) — Long Climbing-Day Simulation
**Modality:** Extended combination session — stair climber + incline treadmill + optional ski erg (from Week 9)
**Primary zone:** Zone 2 (sustained, with natural drift toward Zone 3 on harder segments)

This session is the centrepiece of the climbing-day preparation. It progressively builds toward a session that genuinely simulates the cardiovascular and musculoskeletal demands of a long day out. The combination of modalities, the sustained duration, and the postural demands of maintaining good form under fatigue are all directly transferable.

**Week 9:**
55 minutes continuous. Structure: 25 minutes stair climber (Zone 2, moderate step rate), 5 minutes easy transition walk on treadmill (Zone 1), 25 minutes incline treadmill walk (10–12% incline, Zone 2). The 5-minute transition mimics the rest periods between climbs — she keeps moving but at a lower intensity. Optionally, introduce 10 minutes on the ski erg at the end of the stair climber portion if she has been cleared and has been tolerating the strength programme without shoulder issues. Monitor carefully.

**Week 10:**
60 minutes continuous. Structure: 25 minutes stair climber, 5 minutes easy transition, 30 minutes incline treadmill. Alternatively, if the ski erg has been introduced successfully: 20 minutes stair climber, 10 minutes ski erg (low intensity, Zone 2), 5 minutes transition, 25 minutes incline treadmill.

**Week 11:**
65 minutes continuous. This is the longest single cardio session of the programme and represents a genuine simulation of a moderate climbing day's cardiovascular demand. Structure: 30 minutes stair climber, 5 minutes transition, 30 minutes incline treadmill. Encourage her to treat this session mentally as a climbing day — pack a small bag, bring snacks, hydrate as she would on the hill. The psychological preparation for long days is as important as the physical preparation.

**Week 12 — Final Week:**
35 minutes easy. Zone 1–2 only. Taper. She should feel fresh, capable, and ready to climb.

## Nutrition Integration for Cardio Sessions

The cardio sessions add meaningful caloric expenditure that must be accounted for in the nutrition plan. The following adjustments integrate with the macronutrient targets already established.

### Fuelling Cardio Sessions

**Sessions under 45 minutes (Phase 1 and deload weeks):** No additional fuelling required beyond the standard meal timing already in place. Ensure she has eaten a balanced meal containing carbohydrates and protein within 2–3 hours before the session.

**Sessions 45–60 minutes (Phase 2 and Phase 3 Session 1):** Add 30–40 g of carbohydrates to the pre-session meal. A banana, a small bowl of oats, or a slice of wholegrain toast with honey are all appropriate. No mid-session fuelling required for sessions under 60 minutes if she is well-fed beforehand.

**Sessions over 60 minutes (Phase 3 Session 2, Weeks 10–11):** These sessions are long enough to benefit from mid-session carbohydrate intake. Bring 20–30 g of easily digestible carbohydrates to consume at the 30–35 minute mark — a small banana, a handful of dates, or a rice cake with honey. This directly mimics the snacking behaviour needed on a long climbing day and trains the gut to absorb carbohydrates during sustained exercise, which is a trainable adaptation. Post-session, consume a full meal with protein and carbohydrates within 60–90 minutes.

### Caloric Adjustment for Cardio Days

The cardio sessions burn approximately 250–400 kcal per session depending on duration, intensity, and her bodyweight. On cardio days (Tuesday and Thursday), add 150–200 kcal to the rest-day targets established in the nutrition plan, primarily from carbohydrates. This prevents under-fuelling without eliminating the modest caloric deficit needed for recomposition.

**Revised caloric targets:**

| Day Type | Caloric Target |
|---|---|
| Strength training day (Mon/Wed/Fri) | 2,250–2,300 kcal |
| Cardio day (Tue/Thu) | 1,950–2,050 kcal |

## Recovery Considerations

Adding two cardio sessions to an already demanding three-day strength programme brings the total training days to five per week. This is a meaningful load, particularly in the context of an active injury and a recomposition nutrition strategy. The following recovery practices are non-negotiable components of the programme, not optional extras.

**Sleep:** Seven to nine hours per night is the single most powerful recovery tool available. Growth hormone secretion, muscle protein synthesis, tendon repair, and cardiovascular adaptation all occur predominantly during sleep. If she is consistently sleeping fewer than seven hours, no amount of nutrition or programming optimisation will fully compensate. Address sleep hygiene proactively — consistent sleep and wake times, a cool and dark room, limiting screens in the hour before bed, and the magnesium glycinate supplement in the evening (already included in the nutrition plan) all support sleep quality.

**Saturday active recovery:** Rather than complete rest, a 20–30 minute easy walk outdoors on Saturday is beneficial. It promotes blood flow to recovering tissues, maintains the aerobic adaptations built during the week, and — if done in a natural environment — has well-documented benefits for psychological recovery and stress reduction. This is particularly relevant for a climber, who likely finds outdoor movement intrinsically motivating. Keep it genuinely easy: Zone 1, flat terrain, no pack.

**Foam rolling and mobility:** 10 minutes of foam rolling targeting the thoracic spine, glutes, hip flexors, and calves after each cardio session will reduce delayed onset muscle soreness and maintain the mobility needed for climbing movement. Avoid aggressive foam rolling directly over the shoulder joint.

**Heart rate variability monitoring:** If she has access to a wearable device that measures heart rate variability (HRV), encourage her to track it. A declining HRV trend over several days is an early warning sign of accumulated fatigue and overreaching, and should prompt a reduction in training intensity before symptoms become apparent. This is a sophisticated tool but increasingly accessible through consumer wearables.

## Critical Preamble: Hangboard Training and the Injured Shoulder

This section requires the most careful reading of anything in this programme. Hangboard training is one of the most effective tools in a climber's training arsenal, but it is also one of the most demanding on the shoulder girdle. A dead hang from a hangboard loads the shoulder in passive distraction — the bodyweight pulls the humeral head inferiorly in the glenoid socket, placing significant stress on the superior labrum, the rotator cuff, and the subacromial structures. For a client with active subacromial impingement, this is not a position to rush into.

The approach taken here is deliberately conservative and phased. Hangboard work does not begin until Phase 2 at the earliest, and even then it begins with positions and loads that are far removed from the provocative overhead or fully-loaded hanging positions. Every progression is contingent on the previous step being pain-free — not just during the session, but for 24–48 hours afterward. Night pain, anterior shoulder aching after a session, or any discomfort during the hang itself are all stop signals that require a step back and a conversation with her physiotherapist before continuing.

Share this entire section with her physiotherapist before implementing it. The physio's clinical assessment of her current tissue tolerance is more valuable than any general programme, and their sign-off on each phase transition is strongly recommended.

## Equipment Required

**Hangboard:** A commercially available fingerboard mounted at an appropriate height. The board should be mounted so that when she hangs with arms fully extended, her feet are off the ground but she can step onto a box or chair to take weight off instantly. This is non-negotiable for safety — she must be able to unload the shoulder immediately at any point. Recommended boards for a rehabilitation context include those with large, comfortable edges (at least 35–40 mm depth) and a variety of hold types. Avoid campus rungs or very small crimps until she is fully cleared.

**Pulley system or weight-relief setup:** A simple pulley system (a rope through a carabiner attached to a beam, with a harness or waist loop) allows her to hang with a percentage of her bodyweight supported. This is essential for the early phases of hangboard work and allows precise load management. Alternatively, a box or step that she can partially stand on achieves the same effect less precisely but adequately.

**Resistance bands:** Heavy resistance bands looped around the hangboard and under her feet provide an alternative weight-relief method and are widely used in climbing rehabilitation.

**Climbing shoes:** Not required for hangboard work but useful for the movement preparation exercises introduced in Phase 3.

## Phase 1: Climbing-Specific Preparation Without Hangboard (Weeks 1–4)

### Rationale

There is no hangboard work in Phase 1. The shoulder is not yet ready for hanging loads, and attempting to rush this will set the programme back significantly. However, there is a great deal of climbing-specific preparation that can be done without loading the shoulder at all. Phase 1 climbing prep focuses on three areas: the movement patterns and body awareness that underpin good climbing technique, the foot and lower-body strength that experienced climbers know separates good climbers from great ones, and the mental and tactical skills that can be developed away from the wall entirely.

---

### Phase 1 Climbing Prep Sessions

These are not additional training sessions — they are integrated into the existing schedule as 15–20 minute additions to the end of two strength sessions per week (recommended: Monday and Friday), or as standalone 20-minute sessions on Saturday morning before the active recovery walk. Keep them light and skill-focused.

**1. Footwork and Balance Drills (all phases, ongoing)**

Precise footwork is the foundation of efficient climbing and is entirely shoulder-independent. Poor footwork forces climbers to over-rely on their arms, which is a primary driver of shoulder overuse injuries. Improving her footwork now will directly reduce shoulder loading when she returns to climbing.

*Drill 1 — Quiet Feet on Balance Board or BOSU:*
Stand on a BOSU ball or balance board and practice placing the feet with precision and silence. The goal is to develop proprioceptive awareness in the feet and ankles that translates directly to precise foot placements on small holds. 3 sets × 60 seconds. Progress by closing the eyes in Week 3.

*Drill 2 — Single-Leg Balance with Hip Engagement:*
Stand on one leg on a flat surface, then progress to a slightly unstable surface. Hold for 30–60 seconds each side. Add a slight forward lean from the hips (mimicking the body position over a foothold on a slab) in Week 2. This trains the hip abductors and the proprioceptive chain from foot to hip that is essential for trusting feet on small holds.

*Drill 3 — Step-Up Precision:*
Using a low box (20–30 cm), practice stepping up with precise foot placement — placing the ball of the foot exactly on the edge of the box, as if placing on a small climbing hold. 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Focus on the quality of the placement, not the speed.

**2. Hip Mobility and Flagging Preparation**

High steps, drop knees, and flags are fundamental climbing movements that require significant hip mobility and stability. Developing these now means she can execute them efficiently when she returns to the wall, reducing the compensatory shoulder loading that occurs when climbers cannot use their hips effectively.

*Hip 90/90 Stretch:* Seated on the floor with both legs bent to 90° in front and to the side. Hold the forward position for 60 seconds each side, then rotate to the other side. 3 rounds. This develops the hip external and internal rotation needed for drop knees and high steps.

*Lateral Lunge with Hip Shift:* Standing, take a wide lateral step and shift the hips back and to the side, keeping the stepping foot flat. This mimics the hip position of a drop knee. 3 sets × 10 reps each side.

*Standing Hip Circle:* Standing on one leg, draw large circles with the raised knee — forward, out, back, in. 10 circles each direction, each side. Develops hip mobility in all planes relevant to climbing movement.

**3. Core-to-Extremity Tension Patterns**

Climbing requires the ability to transmit force from the feet through the core to the hands — what coaches call body tension. Weak body tension means the climber sags away from the wall, dramatically increasing the load on the arms and shoulders. Building body tension now is one of the highest-leverage things she can do for her shoulder health as a climber.

*Hollow Body Hold:* Lying on the back, press the lower back into the floor, lift the legs to 45° and the shoulders slightly off the floor, arms by the sides. Hold for 20–30 seconds. This is the fundamental body tension position. 3 sets. Progress to arms extended overhead (but this is a shoulder position — keep arms by the sides for Phase 1).

*Dead Bug (arms at sides, leg extension only):* Lying on the back in hollow body position, extend one leg toward the floor without touching it, return, alternate. 3 sets × 10 reps each side. Trains the anti-extension core stability that underpins body tension on overhanging terrain.

*Plank with Scapular Protraction:* Standard forearm plank, but actively push the floor away with the forearms to protract the scapulae. This is a serratus anterior exercise in a climbing-relevant position. 3 sets × 30–45 second holds. This bridges the gap between the scapular exercises in the strength programme and the demands of climbing movement.

**4. Mental Skills and Tactical Preparation**

Long climbing days are as much a mental challenge as a physical one. Use Phase 1 to develop the mental skills that will make her return to climbing more effective and enjoyable.

*Route reading practice:* Watch climbing videos (YouTube, UKClimbing, The Circuit Climbing) and practice reading routes before watching the climber attempt them. Identify rest positions, foot sequences, and crux sections. This is a genuine skill that improves with deliberate practice and requires no physical loading whatsoever.

*Breathing practice:* Climbers frequently hold their breath on hard moves, which accelerates fatigue and increases perceived exertion. Practice diaphragmatic breathing during the hollow body holds and dead bugs — inhale for 4 counts, exhale for 6 counts. This trains the habit of breathing through effort that will transfer directly to climbing performance.

## Phase 2: Hangboard Introduction and Climbing Prep Development (Weeks 5–8)

### Rationale

By Week 5, she has four weeks of structured shoulder strengthening, scapular control work, and body tension training behind her. The shoulder should be demonstrating improved stability and pain-free range. This is the appropriate point to introduce the hangboard — but the introduction is extremely gradual and begins with positions that are far from the provocative overhead hang.

**Before beginning any hangboard work in Week 5, confirm the following:**
- Zero pain during all Phase 1 strength exercises
- Zero night pain in the right shoulder
- Physiotherapist is aware and supportive of hangboard introduction
- She can perform the scapular depression hold (from the strength programme) for 15 seconds without discomfort
- She can perform a dead hang from the pull-up bar (introduced in Phase 3 of the strength programme, Week 9) — if this has not yet been introduced, do not begin hangboard work until it has been established

If any of these conditions are not met, delay hangboard introduction by one week and reassess.

---

### Hangboard Session Placement

Hangboard sessions are added to two of the existing strength sessions per week — specifically, they are performed at the end of Session A (Monday) and Session C (Friday), after the main strength work is complete. They add approximately 15–20 minutes to these sessions. Do not add hangboard work to the cardio days or as standalone sessions — the total training load is already significant and recovery must be protected.

---

### Week 5: Hangboard Introduction — Assisted Hanging

**Setup:** Use a pulley system or heavy resistance band to support 40–50% of her bodyweight. She should be hanging with a load equivalent to roughly half her bodyweight through the shoulder. This is a very conservative starting point and is intentional.

**Hold type:** Open-hand grip on the largest, most comfortable edge available (35–40 mm minimum). The open-hand grip (fingers slightly bent, not fully crimped) is safer for the finger tendons and produces less shoulder internal rotation than a full crimp. Do not use crimps, slopers, or pinches in Phase 2.

**Position:** Arms fully extended, scapulae actively depressed (she should be actively pulling her shoulder blades down, not passively hanging). This active scapular depression is critical — it engages the lower trapezius and serratus anterior, reduces subacromial compression, and is the correct motor pattern for climbing. Passive hanging with elevated scapulae is provocative for impingement and must be avoided throughout the programme.

**Protocol — Week 5:**
3 sets × 7-second hangs on each hand position, with 3 minutes rest between sets. Begin with both hands on the large edge. Focus entirely on the quality of the hang — active scapular depression, relaxed neck, even weight distribution through both hands. Monitor the right shoulder carefully during and after each set. If any discomfort arises, stop immediately.

Total hangboard volume: 3 sets × 7 seconds = 21 seconds of hanging. This is deliberately minimal. The goal is tissue adaptation, not fatigue.

**Climbing prep additions in Week 5:**

*Tension Board or System Wall Body Tension Work (if available):*
If the gym has a tension board or system wall, introduce low-angle (slab or vertical) movement with feet only — no hands on holds, just walking the feet up the wall while the hands rest lightly on the surface for balance. This develops foot precision and body positioning on the wall without any shoulder loading. 10–15 minutes of exploratory movement.

*Hip Flexor Strength for High Steps:*
Add hanging knee raises (from the pull-up bar, both hands, controlled) — 3 sets × 10 reps. This directly trains the hip flexor strength needed for high steps and is also a gentle introduction to hanging from the bar with active shoulder engagement. Monitor the right shoulder.

---

### Week 6: Hangboard Progression — Increased Duration and Grip Variety

**Protocol:**
Reduce assistance to 30–35% of bodyweight (slightly more load through the shoulder than Week 5).
4 sets × 7-second hangs on the large edge, both hands. Rest 3 minutes between sets.
Add 2 sets × 7-second hangs on a medium edge (25–30 mm) at the end, still with assistance. Rest 3 minutes.

Total volume: 6 sets × 7 seconds = 42 seconds of hanging.

**Climbing prep additions in Week 6:**

*Footwork on the Wall — Slab Traversing:*
If the gym has a climbing wall, introduce low-angle traversing (slab or vertical, maximum 5° overhang) with a focus on footwork only. She can use her hands for balance but should not pull with the arms. Keep the right shoulder in a relaxed, unloaded position throughout. 10 minutes of traversing with deliberate, precise foot placements. This is the first time she is back on the wall — treat it as a significant milestone and monitor her shoulder response carefully for 24–48 hours afterward.

*Drop Knee Practice on the Wall:*
On a vertical section of wall, practice the drop knee position — place one foot on a hold, rotate the knee inward and downward, and feel the hip engagement. No arm loading. This is a technique drill, not a climbing session.

---

### Week 7: Hangboard Progression — Unilateral Introduction

**Protocol:**
Reduce assistance to 20–25% of bodyweight.
4 sets × 10-second hangs on the large edge, both hands. Rest 3 minutes.
2 sets × 7-second hangs on the medium edge, both hands. Rest 3 minutes.
Introduce 2 sets × 5-second single-arm assisted hangs on the right hand (large edge, 50% assistance). This is the first time the right shoulder is loaded in isolation in a hanging position. Be extremely conservative — 50% assistance means only half her bodyweight is going through the right shoulder. Monitor very carefully. Rest 3 minutes between sets.

Total volume: 8 sets of hanging, approximately 65 seconds total.

**Climbing prep additions in Week 7:**

*Vertical Wall Climbing — Easy Routes:*
If the shoulder has been responding well to the hangboard work and the physiotherapist is supportive, introduce easy climbing on vertical or slightly less-than-vertical terrain. Grade should be well within her ability — the goal is movement quality, not difficulty. Limit to 20–30 minutes of easy climbing. She should be able to climb without any shoulder discomfort and should stop immediately if any arises. This is a significant milestone — celebrate it appropriately.

*Route Reading on the Wall:*
Before each easy climb, spend 2–3 minutes reading the route from the ground. Identify the rest positions, the foot sequences, and the body positions. Then climb with the intention of executing the plan. This develops the tactical intelligence that makes long climbing days more efficient and less physically demanding.

---

### Week 8 (Deload): Hangboard and Climbing Prep Deload

Reduce hangboard volume by 50%. 3 sets × 7-second hangs on the large edge, both hands, with 30% assistance. No single-arm work. No new climbing. Use this week to consolidate the movement patterns introduced in Weeks 5–7 and allow the finger tendons and shoulder to recover. Finger tendons adapt more slowly than muscles — they require longer recovery periods and respond poorly to aggressive loading. The deload week is as important for tendon health as it is for muscle recovery.
