## Phase 3: Progressive Hangboard Loading and Return-to-Climbing Protocol (Weeks 9–12)

### Rationale

Phase 3 is where the programme comes together. The shoulder has been progressively loaded for eight weeks, the aerobic base is well-developed, the body tension and footwork foundations are in place, and the finger tendons have been introduced to hanging loads. The goal now is to build genuine finger strength, progress toward unassisted hanging, and establish a structured return-to-climbing protocol that sets her up for long climbing days safely and sustainably.

---

### Hangboard Session Structure in Phase 3

Hangboard sessions remain attached to Monday and Friday strength sessions. They now expand to 25–30 minutes and include a more structured warm-up protocol, as the loads are becoming meaningful.

**Hangboard Warm-Up Protocol (5 minutes, every session from Week 9 onward):**
This warm-up is non-negotiable. Finger tendons and pulleys are avascular structures that warm up slowly and are vulnerable to injury when loaded cold.

Begin with 2 minutes of easy squeezing of a soft stress ball or therapy putty to increase blood flow to the fingers and forearms. Follow with 2 sets × 10-second assisted hangs (40% assistance) on the largest edge available — these are warm-up hangs, not working sets, and should feel very easy. Finish with 10 gentle finger extensions against a rubber band (place a rubber band around all five fingers and open the hand against resistance) to balance the flexor-dominant loading of hanging.

---

### Week 9: Hangboard — Reduced Assistance and Increased Volume

**Protocol:**
Reduce assistance to 15% of bodyweight (approaching unassisted hanging).

*Set 1–4:* 10-second hangs on large edge (35–40 mm), both hands, 15% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 5–6:* 10-second hangs on medium edge (25 mm), both hands, 15% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 7–8:* 7-second single-arm hangs, right hand, large edge, 30% assistance (more conservative on the injured side). Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 9–10:* 7-second single-arm hangs, left hand, large edge, 15% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.

Total volume: 10 sets, approximately 90 seconds of hanging.

**Grip position progression:** Introduce the half-crimp position on the large edge in sets 1–4. The half-crimp (fingers bent to approximately 90° at the proximal interphalangeal joint, thumb not wrapped) is the most commonly used grip position in climbing and produces less tendon stress than the full crimp. Do not use full crimp (thumb wrapped over index finger) until Phase 3 Week 11 at the earliest, and only if all other positions are pain-free.

---

### Week 9: Climbing Prep — Structured Wall Sessions

**Wall Session Structure (2 sessions per week, replacing one cardio session and one rest day — or added to Saturday if energy allows):**

By Week 9, she should be returning to the climbing wall in a structured way. These are not free climbing sessions — they are deliberate practice sessions with specific objectives.

**Wall Session 1 — Technique and Footwork (45–60 minutes):**

*Warm-up (10 minutes):* Easy traversing on vertical terrain, well below her limit. Focus on quiet feet and relaxed arms.

*Main work — 4×4 Footwork Drill (15 minutes):* Choose four easy routes or boulder problems. Climb each one four times consecutively, focusing on a different footwork cue each round: Round 1 — precise placement (place the ball of the foot exactly on the hold), Round 2 — silent feet (no scraping or readjusting), Round 3 — weight transfer (fully commit weight to each foot before moving the hands), Round 4 — look at every foothold before placing the foot. Rest 3 minutes between each set of four climbs.

*Main work — Body Tension Traversing (15 minutes):* Traverse a section of wall on vertical or slightly overhanging terrain, focusing on maintaining body tension throughout. She should feel her core engaged and her hips close to the wall at all times. If she feels herself sagging away from the wall, she is either too tired or the terrain is too steep — reduce the angle.

*Cool-down (10 minutes):* Easy climbing on slab terrain. Gentle forearm stretching and shoulder mobility work.

**Wall Session 2 — Endurance and Route Climbing (45–60 minutes):**

*Warm-up (10 minutes):* Same as Session 1.

*Main work — Pyramid Climbing (20 minutes):* Climb a series of routes in a pyramid structure — start with two routes at a comfortable grade, then one route one grade harder, then back down to two routes at the comfortable grade. The goal is sustained movement with adequate rest, not pushing to failure. Rest 5 minutes between routes.

*Main work — Sustained Traversing (15 minutes):* Traverse continuously for 4-minute periods with 2 minutes rest. This directly trains the aerobic endurance needed for long climbing days. Keep the terrain easy enough that she can maintain movement for the full 4 minutes without pumping out.

*Cool-down (10 minutes):* Same as Session 1.

---

### Week 10: Hangboard — Approaching Unassisted Hanging

**Protocol:**
Reduce assistance to 10% of bodyweight on bilateral hangs. Right arm single-arm hangs remain at 25% assistance.

*Set 1–4:* 10-second hangs, large edge, both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 5–6:* 10-second hangs, medium edge (25 mm), both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 7–8:* 10-second hangs, large edge, half-crimp, both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 9–10:* 7-second single-arm hangs, right hand, large edge, 25% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
*Set 11–12:* 10-second single-arm hangs, left hand, large edge, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.

Total volume: 12 sets, approximately 110 seconds of hanging.

**Introduce repeaters protocol (both hands only):**
Repeaters are the most widely used hangboard protocol in climbing training. The standard format is 7 seconds on, 3 seconds off, repeated 6 times per set, with 3 minutes rest between sets. Introduce one set of repeaters on the large edge at 15% assistance. This is a significant increase in time under tension compared to single hangs — monitor forearm fatigue and shoulder response carefully.

**Week 10 Climbing Prep:**

*Wall Session 1 — Movement Quality on Steeper Terrain:*
Introduce slightly overhanging terrain (up to 15° overhang) for the first time. Keep grades easy. The focus is on maintaining body tension and hip engagement on steeper ground — the positions that are most demanding on the shoulder when technique breaks down. Monitor the right shoulder carefully on any move that requires the arm to be extended above shoulder height.

*Wall Session 2 — Longer Routes and Pacing:*
Focus on pacing — climbing at a speed that allows her to rest on the route, shake out the forearms, and recover between hard moves. This is a critical skill for long climbing days. Choose routes with obvious rest positions and practice identifying and using them.

---

### Week 11: Hangboard — First Unassisted Bilateral Hangs

This is a significant milestone. Week 11 introduces the first fully unassisted bilateral hangs — her full bodyweight through both shoulders on the hangboard. This should only proceed if all previous hangboard work has been completely pain-free and her physiotherapist is supportive.

**Protocol:**

*Warm-up sets (2 sets):* 10-second hangs, large edge, both hands, 10% assistance. These are warm-up sets only.

*Working sets 1–3:* 7-second hangs, large edge (35–40 mm), both hands, NO assistance. Full bodyweight. Rest 3 minutes. Monitor the right shoulder during and after each set. If any discomfort arises, reintroduce 10% assistance and do not progress further this week.

*Working sets 4–6:* 7-second hangs, medium edge (25 mm), both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.

# Phase 3 Revised: Peak Performance Protocol
### Week 12 Climbing Trip Target | Full Programme Integration

## Reframing Phase 3 Completely

The original Phase 3 was built on a conservative linear progression toward readiness. That framing changes now. She has a hard deadline — a climbing trip in Week 12 — and everything in the final four weeks must be organised around arriving at that trip in the best possible physical condition: strong, fit, finger-strong, well-fuelled, psychologically sharp, and with a shoulder that has been progressively loaded to tolerate a full day on the wall or crag without breaking down.

This requires a genuine periodisation shift. In strength and conditioning terms, she needs to peak — a deliberate process of accumulating high training stress in Weeks 9 and 10, beginning to convert that stress into expressed performance in Week 11, and then tapering sharply in Week 12 so that she arrives at the trip recovered, supercompensated, and ready to perform at her best. Peaking is not simply training hard until the day of the event. Done incorrectly, it produces a fatigued, overtrained athlete who performs below their potential. Done correctly, it produces a window of 5–10 days where fitness, recovery, and readiness align simultaneously.

The shoulder remains the governing constraint throughout. Pushing intensity does not mean ignoring the injury — it means being smarter about where intensity is applied, how recovery is managed, and how the taper is structured to protect the shoulder while maximising fitness expression. Any session that produces shoulder pain above 1/10 is modified immediately. The trip is the goal, and arriving injured defeats the entire purpose.

## Week 9: Accumulation I — Building the Peak

### Training Philosophy This Week

Week 9 is the first of two high-load accumulation weeks. The goal is to drive a significant adaptive stimulus across all systems simultaneously — strength, finger strength, aerobic capacity, and climbing movement quality. She will feel fatigued by the end of this week. That is appropriate and expected. The fatigue is the stimulus. Recovery in Weeks 11 and 12 will convert that stimulus into expressed performance.

Total training days this week: five. Monday, Wednesday, Friday strength; Tuesday cardio; Thursday cardio. Hangboard is attached to Monday and Friday strength sessions. Wall sessions begin this week on Saturday, replacing the active recovery walk.

---

### Monday — Strength Session A + Hangboard

**Warm-up (12 minutes)**
5 minutes arm-bike at moderate resistance, building from Zone 1 to Zone 2 by minute 4. Then 3 rounds of: 10 band pull-aparts, 8 face pulls with light band, 10 scapular wall slides to pain-free range, 10 prone Y-raises with 1 kg.

**Main Strength Work**

*A1. Barbell Bent-Over Row* — 5 sets × 5 reps at 87–90% of her current working maximum. This is genuinely heavy — she should need the full 3-minute rest between sets and should not be able to hold a conversation during the set. Maintain perfect scapular mechanics throughout. If form breaks down on the fifth rep of any set, reduce load by 5% for the remaining sets. Do not sacrifice technique for load.

*A2. Neutral-Grip Pull-Down* — 4 sets × 5 reps, heavy. Same loading philosophy as the row. Initiate every rep with scapular depression before the elbow bends. Rest 2.5 minutes.

*A3. Face Pull* — 4 sets × 15 reps. Load is moderate — this is shoulder health maintenance, not a strength exercise at this point in the programme. Never sacrifice the face pull for time or fatigue. Rest 60 seconds.

*A4. Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row* — 3 sets × 8 reps, heavier than Week 8. Rest 90 seconds.

**Accessory Superset (performed as a circuit, 2 rounds, 30 seconds rest between exercises, 90 seconds between rounds)**
Prone lower trap raise (3 kg) × 10, band pull-apart × 20, side-lying external rotation right side × 12.

**Hangboard Block (after 10-minute rest following strength work)**

*Warm-up hangs:* 2 sets × 10-second assisted hangs (20% assistance), large edge, both hands. Rest 2 minutes.

*Working sets:*
Sets 1–4: 10-second hangs, large edge (35–40 mm), open hand, both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
Sets 5–6: 10-second hangs, medium edge (25 mm), half-crimp, both hands, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
Sets 7–8: 7-second single-arm hangs, right hand, large edge, 25% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
Sets 9–10: 10-second single-arm hangs, left hand, large edge, 10% assistance. Rest 3 minutes.
Sets 11–12: Repeaters — 7 seconds on, 3 seconds off × 6 reps, large edge, 15% assistance. Rest 3 minutes between sets.

*Post-hangboard:* 5 minutes forearm stretching. Wrist flexor stretch (arm extended, palm up, gently pull fingers back), wrist extensor stretch (arm extended, palm down, gently press fingers down), prayer stretch, reverse prayer stretch. These are non-negotiable — forearm flexibility is a limiting factor in climbing performance and is frequently neglected.

---

### Tuesday — Cardio Session 1: High-Intensity Intervals

**Modality:** Stair climber
**Total session:** 42 minutes

Warm-up: 5 minutes Zone 1, building pace gradually.

Main work: 7 rounds of the following sequence — 3 minutes Zone 2 (RPE 5–6, sustainable pace), 90 seconds Zone 3 (RPE 7–8, hard but controlled), 30 seconds Zone 4 (RPE 9–10, maximum effort). The Zone 4 efforts should be genuinely maximal — she should not be able to speak and should feel significant cardiovascular stress. The 3-minute Zone 2 recovery between rounds is active and should feel restorative by the end of the 3 minutes. If she is not recovering adequately between rounds, extend the Zone 2 period to 4 minutes rather than reducing the intensity of the hard efforts.

Cool-down: 5 minutes Zone 1.

This session is demanding. Ensure she has eaten a carbohydrate-containing meal within 2 hours before and consumes 30–40 g of carbohydrates within 60 minutes after.

---

### Wednesday — Strength Session B

**Warm-up** — Same as Monday.

**Main Strength Work**

*A1. Dumbbell Bench Press (neutral grip, flat bench)* — 5 sets × 5 reps, heavy. This is the heaviest pressing she will do in the programme. Monitor the bottom position of the press carefully — if the right shoulder reports any discomfort as the dumbbells descend, place a folded towel under the right side of the bench to limit range, or reduce load. Rest 3 minutes.

# Mobility Programme
### Fully Integrated with Strength, Cardio, Hangboard & Nutrition Plan | Right Subacromial Impingement

---

## Programming Philosophy

Mobility work for this client serves four distinct purposes that must be held simultaneously. The first is direct injury management — restoring and maintaining the range of motion in the right shoulder that impingement progressively restricts, particularly posterior capsule tightness and internal rotation deficit, which are almost universally present in this presentation and are considered by many shoulder specialists to be a primary mechanical driver of subacromial impingement rather than merely a consequence of it. The second is climbing performance — climbers require exceptional mobility in the thoracic spine, hips, and shoulders to execute efficient movement, and restrictions in any of these areas force compensatory loading patterns that increase injury risk. The third is training longevity — five training days per week across strength, cardio, hangboard, and wall sessions creates significant tissue stress, and mobility work is the primary tool for managing that stress and keeping her training consistently across the full 12 weeks. The fourth is peak preparation — arriving at the Week 12 climbing trip with full, pain-free range of motion in every relevant joint is as important as arriving strong and fit.

Mobility work is not stretching in the traditional sense, and this distinction matters practically. Static stretching held passively for 30–60 seconds produces temporary range of motion improvements that do not reliably transfer to movement under load. What produces lasting, functional mobility improvements is a combination of controlled articular rotations that explore end-range positions actively, loaded progressive stretching that teaches the nervous system to trust new ranges, and dynamic movement that integrates mobility into the patterns she actually uses in climbing. All three approaches are used in this programme.

The right shoulder receives specific, targeted mobility work throughout all 12 weeks. The thoracic spine receives consistent attention because thoracic kyphosis and stiffness are the single most common postural driver of subacromial impingement — a rounded upper back tilts the scapula forward and downward, reducing the subacromial space and making impingement mechanically inevitable regardless of how strong the rotator cuff is. The hips receive progressive mobility work that builds toward the high steps, drop knees, and flags that define efficient climbing movement. The wrists and fingers receive specific preparation for hangboard loading from Phase 2 onward.

---

## Mobility Session Placement

Mobility work is integrated into the existing programme in three ways. Daily maintenance mobility takes 8–10 minutes and is performed every morning before anything else — it is the non-negotiable foundation of the programme and should be treated with the same seriousness as the training sessions themselves. Post-session mobility is performed at the end of every training session and replaces the cool-down sections already described in the programme — it is more structured and purposeful than the general cool-down work previously outlined. Dedicated mobility sessions are 25–30 minute standalone sessions performed on Saturday and Sunday, replacing the general active recovery description previously given for those days.

| Time | Mobility Component | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Every morning | Daily maintenance routine | 8–10 min |
| End of every training session | Post-session targeted mobility | 10–15 min |
| Saturday | Dedicated full-body mobility session | 25–30 min |
| Sunday | Dedicated recovery mobility session | 20–25 min |

## The Daily Maintenance Routine (Every Morning, All 12 Weeks)

This routine is performed immediately upon waking, before coffee, before checking a phone, before anything else. It takes 8–10 minutes. Its purpose is to restore the range of motion that sleep compresses — the shoulder capsule tightens overnight, the thoracic spine stiffens in whatever position she slept in, and the hips lose the mobility work accumulated the previous day if it is not reinforced. Performing this routine consistently is more valuable than any single dedicated mobility session done sporadically.

The routine never changes across all 12 weeks. Consistency is the mechanism — the nervous system learns to trust these ranges through repeated daily exposure, not through occasional intensive sessions.

**1. Thoracic Rotation in 90/90 Position (2 minutes)**
Lie on the right side with both hips and knees bent to 90°, a pillow or folded towel between the knees to keep the hips stacked. Both arms extended in front of the chest at shoulder height. Keeping the hips completely still and the knees together, rotate the top arm (left arm) open toward the ceiling and as far toward the floor on the other side as it will go without the hips rolling. Follow the hand with the eyes and head. Hold the end position for 3 slow breaths — inhale through the nose for 4 counts, exhale through the mouth for 6 counts. Return slowly. Perform 8 repetitions on the left side (opening the chest), then switch to lie on the left side and perform 8 repetitions opening the right arm. The right side will likely have less range than the left — do not force it. Work to the comfortable end range and breathe into it.

This is the single most important exercise in the entire mobility programme for her injury. Posterior shoulder tightness and thoracic rotation restriction are the two most consistent mechanical findings in subacromial impingement, and this exercise addresses both simultaneously. Research by Burkhart, Morgan, and Kibler — the group that coined the term SICK scapula syndrome — consistently identifies posterior capsule tightness as a primary driver of the superior migration of the humeral head that causes impingement. Daily work in this position is the most direct intervention available outside of physiotherapy.

**2. Cat-Cow with Thoracic Emphasis (90 seconds)**
On hands and knees, wrists under shoulders, knees under hips. Perform standard cat-cow — exhale and round the entire spine from tailbone to crown (cat), inhale and extend the entire spine (cow). After 4 full rounds, begin to isolate the thoracic spine: on the extension phase, try to create the movement specifically in the mid-back rather than the lower back, which tends to dominate. Place one hand behind the head and rotate the elbow toward the ceiling on each extension to increase the thoracic rotation component. 5 repetitions each side. This mobilises the thoracic facet joints that stiffen overnight and directly improves the scapular mechanics that underpin shoulder health.

**3. Hip 90/90 with Forward Fold (2 minutes)**
Sit on the floor with both legs bent to 90° — one leg in front (hip externally rotated) and one leg behind (hip internally rotated). Sit tall and breathe. After 4 breaths, hinge forward over the front leg, keeping the spine long rather than rounding. Hold for 4 breaths. Return upright, then lean toward the back leg. Hold for 4 breaths. Switch sides. This develops the hip external and internal rotation needed for drop knees and high steps in climbing and is one of the most time-efficient hip mobility exercises available.

**4. Doorway or Wall Pec Stretch at 90° (60 seconds each side)**
Stand in a doorway or beside a wall. Place the right forearm vertically on the door frame, elbow at 90°, upper arm parallel to the floor. Gently rotate the body away from the arm until a stretch is felt across the chest and anterior shoulder. Hold for 60 seconds with slow, relaxed breathing. Do not elevate the arm above 90° — this is the provocative range for impingement and must be avoided in this stretch throughout all 12 weeks. Repeat on the left side. This addresses the pectoral tightness that anteriorly tilts the scapula and reduces the subacromial space.

**5. Neck and Upper Trapezius Release (90 seconds)**
Sitting or standing, drop the right ear toward the right shoulder. Place the right hand gently on the left side of the head — not pulling, just adding light weight. Hold for 4 breaths. Then rotate the chin toward the right armpit and hold for 4 breaths. This releases the upper trapezius and levator scapulae, which are chronically overactive in impingement presentations and contribute to the scapular elevation that reduces the subacromial space. Repeat on the other side.

## Post-Session Mobility (After Every Training Session)

The post-session mobility routine is tailored to the type of session just completed. There are three versions — one for strength sessions, one for cardio sessions, and one for wall sessions. Each takes 10–15 minutes.

---

### Post-Strength Session Mobility (10–12 minutes)

Performed immediately after the cool-down at the end of every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday session.

**1. Posterior Shoulder Capsule Stretch — Sleeper Stretch (2 minutes each side)**
Lie on the right side with the right arm extended in front at shoulder height, elbow bent to 90°, forearm pointing toward the ceiling. Using the left hand, gently press the right forearm toward the floor — internally rotating the right shoulder. Stop immediately at any discomfort. The target sensation is a deep stretch in the posterior right shoulder, not pain. Hold for 20 seconds, release, repeat. Perform 4 repetitions on the right side, then switch to the left. This is the most direct intervention for posterior capsule tightness and should be performed after every strength session without exception. Research by McClure and colleagues demonstrates that consistent sleeper stretch practice significantly reduces posterior shoulder tightness and improves internal rotation range of motion in overhead athletes — the same mechanism applies here.

**2. Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller (2 minutes)**
Place a foam roller perpendicular to the spine at the mid-back (thoracic spine, not lumbar). Support the head with both hands. Gently extend over the roller, allowing the thoracic spine to extend around it. Hold for 3 breaths, then move the roller one segment up the spine and repeat. Work from the lower thoracic spine (T12) to the upper thoracic spine (T4) — approximately 5–6 positions. Do not extend the lumbar spine over the roller. This is the most effective tool available for restoring thoracic extension mobility and directly improves scapular upward rotation mechanics.

**3. Doorway Pec Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Same as the daily maintenance version. Reinforces the anterior shoulder mobility work done in the morning.

**4. Cross-Body Posterior Capsule Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Standing or seated, bring the right arm across the body at shoulder height. Use the left hand to gently press the right arm closer to the chest. Hold for 60 seconds with slow breathing. This is a gentler version of the sleeper stretch and targets the same posterior capsule tissue from a different angle.

**5. Wrist Flexor and Extensor Stretch (2 minutes)**
Extend the right arm in front, palm up. Use the left hand to gently pull the fingers back toward the body. Hold for 30 seconds. Then turn the palm down and gently press the fingers toward the body. Hold for 30 seconds. Repeat on the left side. This is essential for climbing preparation and becomes increasingly important as hangboard work begins in Phase 2.

**6. Hip Flexor Stretch — Half-Kneeling (90 seconds each side)**
In a half-kneeling position, tuck the pelvis under (posterior pelvic tilt) and shift the hips forward until a stretch is felt in the front of the rear hip. Hold for 90 seconds each side. Hip flexor tightness is extremely common in people who sit for work and directly limits the high-step range of motion needed for efficient climbing.

---

### Post-Cardio Session Mobility (10 minutes)

Performed after Tuesday and Thursday cardio sessions.

**1. Standing Quad and Hip Flexor Stretch (90 seconds each side)**
Standing on one leg, pull the opposite foot toward the glutes. Tuck the pelvis under to increase the hip flexor component. Hold for 90 seconds each side. The stair climber and incline treadmill create significant hip flexor and quadriceps loading — this stretch directly addresses the resulting tightness.

**2. Pigeon Pose or Figure-Four Stretch (2 minutes each side)**
Pigeon pose on the floor (front shin roughly parallel to the front of the mat, rear leg extended behind) or a supine figure-four stretch (lying on the back, cross one ankle over the opposite knee, pull both legs toward the chest). Hold for 2 minutes each side with slow breathing. This targets the piriformis and deep hip external rotators that are heavily loaded during stair climbing and are directly relevant to drop knee mechanics in climbing.

**3. Calf and Achilles Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Standing facing a wall, place one foot behind the other. Press the rear heel into the floor and lean toward the wall. Hold for 30 seconds (straight knee, targeting gastrocnemius), then slightly bend the rear knee and hold for 30 seconds (targeting soleus and Achilles). Repeat each side. The stair climber creates significant calf loading and approach hiking demands excellent ankle dorsiflexion — this stretch addresses both.

**4. Thoracic Rotation in 90/90 (same as morning routine, 90 seconds each side)**
Reinforce the morning work. The thoracic spine benefits from multiple short mobility sessions throughout the day more than from one long session.

**5. Glute and Piriformis Release on Foam Roller (2 minutes)**
Sit on the foam roller with one ankle crossed over the opposite knee. Roll slowly over the glute and piriformis of the crossed leg. Pause on tender spots for 5–10 seconds. Switch sides. This reduces the muscle tension that accumulates from sustained stair climbing and incline walking.

---

### Post-Wall Session Mobility (15 minutes)

Wall sessions create a unique combination of tissue stress — forearm flexor loading, finger tendon stress, shoulder girdle fatigue, hip loading from high steps and drop knees, and calf loading from standing on small footholds. The post-wall mobility routine addresses all of these.

**1. Forearm Flexor Stretch Sequence (3 minutes)**
Four positions, 45 seconds each, both arms simultaneously where possible:
Position 1 — Prayer stretch: palms together in front of the chest, fingers pointing up, press hands together and lower them toward the waist until a stretch is felt in the forearm flexors.
Position 2 — Reverse prayer: backs of hands together, fingers pointing down, raise hands toward the chest.
Position 3 — Extended arm flexor stretch: arm extended in front, palm up, use the other hand to pull fingers back.
Position 4 — Extended arm extensor stretch: arm extended in front, palm down, use the other hand to press fingers toward the body.

**2. Finger Tendon Mobilisation (2 minutes)**
This is not a stretch — it is a gentle active mobilisation. Make a loose fist, then slowly extend all fingers as wide as possible, spreading them apart. Hold the extended position for 3 seconds. Repeat 10 times. Then perform individual finger circles — gently rotate each finger at the base knuckle in small circles, 5 each direction. This promotes synovial fluid circulation in the finger joints and reduces the stiffness that accumulates after hangboard and wall sessions.

**3. Sleeper Stretch (2 minutes right side, 90 seconds left)**
Same as post-strength version. The right shoulder receives additional time given the injury history. After a wall session, the posterior capsule will have been loaded repeatedly — this stretch is the most important single intervention for managing that load.

**4. Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller (2 minutes)**
Same as post-strength version. Wall climbing creates significant thoracic flexion loading — the extension work directly counteracts this.

**5. Hip 90/90 with Rotation (2 minutes each side)**
Same as morning routine but held longer. After a wall session involving drop knees and high steps, the hip rotators will be significantly loaded and benefit from extended time in the 90/90 position.

**6. Doorway Pec Stretch (90 seconds each side)**
Same as morning and post-strength versions. Three exposures per training day to this stretch is appropriate given the anterior shoulder tightness associated with climbing.

**7. Wrist Circles and Loaded Wrist Mobility (2 minutes)**
Make large, slow circles with both wrists — 10 each direction. Then perform loaded wrist mobility: place both palms flat on the floor in front of the body (tabletop position) and gently rock forward over the wrists, increasing the wrist extension range. Hold the end position for 3 breaths. This directly prepares the wrists for hangboard loading and addresses the wrist extension restriction that develops from sustained gripping.

## Saturday: Dedicated Full-Body Mobility Session (25–30 minutes)

Saturday follows the hardest training days of the week — Friday strength and hangboard, and the wall session that has been added to the schedule. This dedicated session is the most comprehensive mobility work of the week and addresses every major area relevant to her training and climbing goals.

Perform this session in the morning, before any other activity. Move slowly and deliberately. This is not a workout — it is recovery work, and the intention should be calm, focused, and unhurried.

---

**1. Thoracic Spine Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**

*Foam roller thoracic extension (3 minutes):* Same as post-strength version but more thorough — spend longer at each segment, particularly the upper thoracic spine (T4–T6), which is the most commonly restricted region in climbers and the area most directly linked to scapular mechanics.

*Thread the needle (2 minutes each side):* On hands and knees, slide the right arm under the body along the floor, rotating the thoracic spine until the right shoulder and ear rest on the floor. The left arm can reach toward the ceiling to increase the rotation. Hold for 4 slow breaths. Return and repeat. This is one of the most effective thoracic rotation exercises available and directly addresses the rotation restriction that drives impingement.

*Thoracic rotation in 90/90 (3 minutes):* Same as morning routine but with longer holds — 5 breaths at end range rather than 3. By Saturday, the nervous system has had five days of exposure to this range and can tolerate longer holds.

**2. Shoulder Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**

*Sleeper stretch (3 minutes right, 2 minutes left):* Longer holds than post-session versions. The right shoulder receives 3 minutes because Saturday is the appropriate day for the most thorough posterior capsule work of the week.

*Shoulder CARs — Controlled Articular Rotations (3 minutes):* Standing, pin the right shoulder blade against the rib cage with the left hand (to isolate the glenohumeral joint). Slowly rotate the right arm through the largest circle possible while maintaining scapular control — forward, up to pain-free range only (not overhead), back, and down. The movement should be slow, deliberate, and controlled throughout the entire arc. Perform 5 circles in each direction. This is the most sophisticated shoulder mobility exercise in the programme — it explores the full available range of the glenohumeral joint actively, which is the mechanism by which lasting mobility improvements are made. The key word is pain-free range only — do not push into discomfort.

*Doorway pec stretch with breathing (90 seconds each side):* Same as previous versions but add an active breathing component — on each exhale, allow the chest to open slightly further into the stretch. This uses the respiratory system to facilitate a deeper stretch without forcing.

**3. Hip Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**

*Hip 90/90 with all variations (4 minutes):* Begin in the standard 90/90 position. Spend 60 seconds in the base position on each side. Then add the forward fold over the front leg (60 seconds each side). Then add the lateral lean toward the back leg (60 seconds each side). This is the most thorough hip mobility work of the week.

*Deep squat hold (2 minutes):* Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly. Lower into a deep squat, keeping the heels on the floor. Hold for 2 minutes with slow breathing. ## Programming Philosophy

A Saturday finisher session serves a purpose that the rest of this programme does not fully address — it should be genuinely enjoyable. Every other session in this programme has a specific physiological objective: build strength, develop aerobic capacity, load the finger tendons, restore mobility. The Saturday session has all of those things happening incidentally, but the primary objective is that she leaves feeling like an athlete, not a patient. After four months of physiotherapy and a carefully managed return to training, that psychological shift matters enormously for long-term adherence and for her relationship with her body and her sport.

The session is designed around a circuit-and-challenge format that borrows from climbing culture — problems to solve, movements to master, a physical puzzle that rewards skill and coordination as much as raw fitness. It is full-body, meaning the lower body and core carry a significant share of the load and the shoulder is never the limiting factor. It is progressive across the 12 weeks, becoming more demanding and more climbing-specific as her capacity develops. And it is structured so that the mobility session described in the previous section follows it naturally — the finisher creates the tissue demand, the mobility session addresses it.

The shoulder rules do not change on Saturday. No overhead loading, pain-free range only, and she exits any exercise immediately if the right shoulder reports discomfort. The fun is real but the injury management is non-negotiable.

---

## Session Structure Overview

Every Saturday finisher follows the same broad architecture regardless of the phase. What changes across the 12 weeks is the content within each block, the loading, and the complexity of the movements.

**Total duration:** 50–65 minutes of active work, followed by the 25–30 minute dedicated mobility session already described.

| Block | Purpose | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Movement Prep | Activate, mobilise, prepare | 10 min |
| Block A — Skill Challenge | Technique, coordination, problem-solving | 15 min |
| Block B — Strength Circuit | Full-body loaded movement | 15–20 min |
| Block C — Conditioning Finisher | Cardiovascular, competitive, fun | 10–12 min |
| Cool-down into Mobility | Transition to Saturday mobility session | Into 25-min mobility |

## Phase 1 Saturday Finisher (Weeks 1–4)
### Theme: Movement Foundations

The Phase 1 finisher establishes the movement vocabulary for the rest of the programme. The loads are modest, the movements are learnable, and the emphasis is on quality and body awareness. She should leave these sessions feeling capable and energised rather than destroyed.

---

### Movement Prep (10 minutes, same every week in Phase 1)

Begin with 3 minutes of easy movement — walking, light skipping, or gentle jogging in place — to raise the heart rate and body temperature. Follow with the following sequence performed as a flowing circuit with no rest between exercises, repeated twice:

*World's Greatest Stretch (5 each side):* Step forward into a lunge, place the same-side hand on the floor beside the front foot, rotate the opposite arm toward the ceiling (only to pain-free range — do not force the right arm overhead). This single exercise mobilises the hip flexors, thoracic spine, and shoulder simultaneously and is one of the most time-efficient movement prep exercises available.

*Lateral Squat (8 each side):* Wide stance, shift the weight to one side and lower into a lateral squat, keeping the other leg straight. Return to centre and shift to the other side. Develops the hip mobility and lateral strength relevant to climbing footwork.

*Inchworm (6 repetitions):* Stand with feet hip-width apart, hinge forward and walk the hands out to a plank position, hold for 2 seconds, walk the hands back, return to standing. Activates the core, hamstrings, and shoulder stabilisers in a controlled way.

*Scapular Push-Up (10 repetitions):* In a plank position on the hands, keep the arms straight and protract the scapulae (push the floor away, rounding the upper back slightly), then retract them (allow the chest to drop slightly between the shoulder blades). This is a direct serratus anterior activation exercise and bridges the movement prep into the shoulder health work of the main programme.

---

### Block A — Skill Challenge: Balance and Coordination (15 minutes)

**Week 1 — Single-Leg Balance Progression**

Set up three balance challenges in a circuit. She moves through all three, rests 90 seconds, and repeats for 4 rounds. The goal is to improve with each round — this is a skill practice, not a fitness test.

*Station 1 — BOSU Single-Leg Balance (30 seconds each side):* Stand on the flat side of a BOSU ball on one leg. Progress by closing the eyes in round 3. This develops the proprioceptive awareness in the feet and ankles that translates directly to trusting feet on climbing holds.

*Station 2 — Lateral Step-Over (10 each side):* Place a low hurdle or a foam roller on the floor. Step laterally over it with precision — lift the foot high, place it quietly on the other side, bring the trailing foot over. The emphasis is on deliberate, controlled movement rather than speed. This mimics the precision of foot placements on climbing holds.

*Station 3 — Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift (8 each side, bodyweight):* Stand on one leg, hinge forward from the hip, extending the rear leg behind for balance. Return to standing. This develops single-leg hip hinge strength and balance that is directly relevant to high-step movements in climbing.

**Week 2 — Locomotion Patterns**

Replace the balance circuit with a locomotion challenge. Set up a 10-metre space.

*Bear Crawl (10 metres forward, 10 metres backward):* On hands and feet with knees hovering 5 cm off the floor, crawl forward and backward. Keep the hips level and the core engaged. This is a full-body coordination exercise that loads the shoulder in a safe, sub-90° position and develops the contralateral movement patterns that underpin efficient climbing movement. Monitor the right shoulder — if any discomfort arises, replace with a crab walk (hands and feet, hips facing up).

*Lateral Shuffle with Squat (10 metres each direction):* Shuffle laterally for 5 metres, perform a squat, shuffle back. 4 rounds. Develops lateral movement and lower-body power.

*Broad Jump (6 repetitions):* Jump forward as far as possible with both feet, land softly with bent knees, absorb the landing. This introduces explosive lower-body power in a controlled context.

**Week 3 — Agility and Reaction**

Set up 6 cones in a random pattern across a 5-metre square. The trainer calls a cone number and she moves to it as quickly as possible, touches it, and returns to the centre. 8 rounds of 30 seconds on, 30 seconds off. This develops the reactive agility and spatial awareness that are relevant to moving efficiently on a climbing wall. Progress by adding a bodyweight squat at each cone.

**Week 4 (Deload) — Playful Movement**

Replace the structured skill challenge with 15 minutes of free movement exploration. Give her a simple brief: move in as many different ways as possible using only the floor and her bodyweight. Roll, crawl, balance, jump, stretch. No structure, no counting, no performance pressure. This is active play and serves a genuine neurological purpose — novel movement patterns stimulate motor learning and maintain the movement variability that structured training progressively reduces.

---

### Block B — Strength Circuit (15–20 minutes)

**Phase 1 Circuit Structure:** 5 exercises, performed as a circuit with 30 seconds rest between exercises and 2 minutes rest between rounds. 3 rounds. All exercises are full-body and shoulder-friendly.

**Week 1 Circuit:**

*1. Goblet Squat (12 reps, moderate dumbbell):* Hold a dumbbell vertically at the chest with both hands. Squat to depth, keeping the chest tall and the knees tracking over the toes. This is the foundational lower-body strength exercise of the programme and develops the leg strength needed for long approach hikes.

*2. Single-Arm Dumbbell Row (10 reps each side):* Bench-supported, same as the strength programme. The Saturday circuit reinforces the pulling pattern from the weekday sessions.

*3. Reverse Lunge (10 reps each side, bodyweight):* Step backward into a lunge, lower the rear knee toward the floor, return to standing. Develops single-leg strength and hip stability relevant to climbing footwork.

*4. Dumbbell Floor Press (12 reps, moderate load):* Same as the strength programme. Reinforces the pressing pattern in a circuit context.

*5. Plank with Shoulder Tap (10 taps each side):* In a high plank position, lift one hand and tap the opposite shoulder, keeping the hips level. This develops anti-rotation core stability and shoulder stability simultaneously. Monitor the right shoulder — if any discomfort arises, replace with a standard forearm plank.

**Week 2 Circuit:** Same exercises, increase load by 5% on goblet squat and dumbbell row. Add a 2-second pause at the bottom of the goblet squat and the top of the row.

**Week 3 Circuit:** Same structure, increase load by a further 5%. Add a tempo prescription to the reverse lunge: 3 seconds down, 1-second pause at the bottom, 1 second up.

**Week 4 Circuit (Deload):** Reduce to 2 rounds. Reduce load by 20%. Focus on movement quality rather than load.

### Block C — Conditioning Finisher (10–12 minutes)

**Phase 1 Finisher Philosophy:** The conditioning finisher in Phase 1 is aerobic rather than anaerobic. She is adapting to a new training load and the finisher should elevate the heart rate and create a satisfying sense of physical effort without creating excessive fatigue that compromises recovery for the following week.

**Week 1 — Stair Climber Pyramid:**
5 minutes on the stair climber. Minute 1: Zone 1. Minute 2: Zone 2. Minute 3: Zone 3. Minute 4: Zone 2. Minute 5: Zone 1. Simple, effective, and directly relevant to the climbing day preparation goal.

**Week 2 — Bike Sprint Intervals:**
8 minutes on the stationary bike. Alternate 40 seconds at Zone 2 with 20 seconds at Zone 4 (maximum effort sprint). 8 rounds. This is a simple Tabata-inspired format that introduces high-intensity work in a very controlled, shoulder-free context.

**Week 3 — Bodyweight AMRAP (As Many Rounds As Possible):**
8 minutes. Complete as many rounds as possible of: 10 bodyweight squats, 10 reverse lunges (5 each side), 10 push-ups (or incline push-ups if the right shoulder is not yet tolerating full push-ups — hands on a bench reduces the load), 10 jumping jacks. Record the number of rounds completed. This becomes a benchmark that she can beat in later phases.

**Week 4 (Deload) — Easy Bike:**
10 minutes at Zone 1–2 on the stationary bike. Restorative and easy.

## Phase 2 Saturday Finisher (Weeks 5–8)
### Theme: Strength and Climbing Movement

Phase 2 finishers introduce more climbing-specific movement patterns, heavier loading in the strength circuit, and more demanding conditioning work. The skill challenge block begins to incorporate actual climbing movement mechanics.

---

### Movement Prep (10 minutes, same structure as Phase 1 but with progressions)

Replace the inchworm with a *Spiderman Crawl* — same as the inchworm but add a lateral lunge at each hand position, bringing the front foot up beside the hand and rotating the torso open. Replace the scapular push-up with a *Push-Up to Downward Dog* — perform a push-up, then press the hips up and back into a downward dog position, hold for 2 seconds, return to plank. This adds a hamstring and calf stretch component and increases the shoulder stability demand.

---

### Block A — Skill Challenge: Climbing Movement Mechanics (15 minutes)

**Week 5 — Hip Turn and Flag Practice**

Set up a section of wall or use a mirror. Practice the following climbing movement mechanics without a wall, using a chair or low box as a prop:

*Hip turn drill (10 minutes):* Stand facing a wall with both hands on the wall at chest height. Practice rotating the hips to face the wall (as in a hip turn on a climbing route) while keeping the feet in place. Feel the difference in reach when the hips are square versus turned. This is a fundamental movement pattern that dramatically increases reach and reduces arm loading on climbing routes.

*Flag drill (5 minutes):* Stand on one leg beside a wall. Extend the other leg behind and to the side (back flag) or across the body (inside flag) to maintain balance. This develops the balance and hip control needed for flagging on the wall.

**Week 6 — Tension and Opposition**

*Compression block (8 minutes):* Place two smooth boxes or plates on the floor approximately 60 cm apart. Stand with one foot on each, pressing outward against them (compression). Practice maintaining this outward pressure while performing a slow squat. This mimics the compression body position used on certain climbing problems and develops the hip abductor strength and body tension needed for it.

*Opposition pull drill (7 minutes):* Using a TRX or resistance band anchored at chest height, hold the handles and lean back into a slight recline. Practice pulling with one hand while pushing with the other — the opposition of forces that characterises many climbing movements. 3 sets × 8 reps each side.

**Week 7 — Dynamic Movement and Coordination**

*Climbing-inspired movement flow (15 minutes):* Create a floor-based movement sequence that mimics climbing movement patterns: begin standing, step forward into a lunge (high step), rotate the hips (hip turn), reach forward with the opposite hand (reach), step through to the other side, repeat. Perform this as a flowing sequence for 15 metres, then return. 4 rounds. This is essentially a climbing movement kata — a choreographed sequence of movements that develops the motor patterns of climbing in a low-load, high-repetition context.

**Week 8 (Deload) — Free Movement on the Wall**

15 minutes of easy, exploratory movement on the climbing wall at very low grades. No objectives, no counting, no performance pressure. Just movement for the joy of it.

---

### Block B — Strength Circuit (Phase 2)

**Phase 2 Circuit Structure:** 6 exercises, 3 rounds, 30 seconds rest between exercises, 90 seconds rest between rounds. Heavier loads than Phase 1.

**Week 5 Circuit:**

*1. Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift (10 reps, moderate-heavy):* Hinge from the hips, keeping the back flat, lowering the dumbbells along the legs to mid-shin. This develops the posterior chain strength needed for approach hiking and the hip hinge pattern relevant to climbing body positioning.

*2. Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row (10 reps, heavier than Phase 1):* Same as the strength programme. Reinforce the pulling pattern.

*3. Bulgarian Split Squat (8 reps each side, bodyweight or light dumbbells):* Rear foot elevated on a bench, lower into a single-leg squat. This is the most demanding lower-body exercise introduced so far and develops the single-leg strength and hip stability that are directly relevant to climbing footwork and approach hiking on uneven terrain.

*4. Landmine Press (10 reps each side):* Same as the strength programme. Reinforce the pressing pattern in a circuit context.

*5. TRX Fallout (10 reps):* Hold TRX handles at chest height, lean forward and extend the arms in front (keeping them below 90°), then pull back to the start. This is an anti-extension core exercise that loads the shoulder in a safe position and develops the overhead reach stability relevant to climbing. Monitor the right shoulder carefully — if any discomfort arises, reduce the range of the fallout.

*6. Lateral Band Walk (15 steps each direction):* Place a resistance band around the ankles. Maintain a slight squat position and walk laterally, keeping tension in the band throughout. Develops the hip abductor strength that stabilises the pelvis during single-leg climbing movements.

**Weeks 6 and 7:** Increase load by 5% per week on the Romanian deadlift, chest-supported row, and Bulgarian split squat. Add a 2-second pause at the bottom of the Bulgarian split squat from Week 6.

**Week 8 (Deload):** Reduce to 2 rounds, reduce load by 20%.

### Block C — Conditioning Finisher (Phase 2)

**Week 5 — Partner or Solo Benchmark:**
*The Climbing Pyramid:* On the stair climber, complete the following pyramid without stopping: 1 minute Zone 3, 1 minute Zone 2, 2 minutes Zone 3, 1 minute Zone 2, 1 minute Zone 3. Total: 6 minutes. Record her average step rate at Zone 3. This becomes a benchmark for Phase 3.

**Week 6 — Kettlebell or Dumbbell Complex:**
A complex is a series of exercises performed with the same implement without putting it down. Choose a moderate dumbbell weight. Perform: 6 Romanian deadlifts, 6 bent-over rows (each side), 6 reverse lunges (each side), 6 floor presses. That is one round. Rest 90 seconds. Complete 4 rounds. Record the time. The complex format creates significant metabolic demand while keeping the shoulder in safe positions throughout.

**Week 7 — AMRAP Progression:**
Return to the Week 3 AMRAP format but with progressions: replace bodyweight squats with goblet squats (moderate dumbbell), replace standard push-ups with landmine press (10 reps each side), add 10 TRX rows to the circuit. 10 minutes. Beat the Week 3 round count.

**Week 8 (Deload):** 10 minutes easy stair climber at Zone 1–2.

## Phase 3 Saturday Finisher (Weeks 9–12)
### Theme: Peak Performance and Climbing Readiness

Phase 3 finishers are the most demanding sessions of the programme. They are designed to push her cardiovascular and muscular systems hard in a way that is genuinely fun and directly relevant to climbing performance. The skill challenge block incorporates actual wall climbing. The strength circuit uses the heaviest loads of the programme. The conditioning finisher is competitive and challenging.

### Movement Prep (10 minutes, Phase 3 version)

Replace the lateral squat with a *Cossack Squat* — a deep lateral squat that takes the hip into full external rotation at the bottom. Replace the world's greatest stretch with a *Spiderman with Thoracic Rotation* — same as the world's greatest stretch but add a full thoracic rotation at the top, reaching the arm as high as pain-free range allows. Add *Ankle Circles and Calf Raises* (10 each direction, 15 calf raises) to prepare the ankles for the demanding lower-body work ahead.

---

### Block A — Skill Challenge: Wall Climbing (15 minutes)

By Phase 3, she is back on the wall regularly. The Saturday skill challenge block becomes a structured climbing practice session.

**Week 9 — Technique Refinement Under Fatigue**

Perform the skill challenge block after the movement prep but before the strength circuit — this ensures she is climbing when relatively fresh, which is when technique learning is most effective.

*Footwork 4×4 (10 minutes):* Choose four routes or problems at a comfortable grade. Climb each one four times with a specific focus: Round 1 — silent feet, Round 2 — straight arms (keep the arms as straight as possible, using the skeleton rather than the muscles to hang), Round 3 — hip turns on every move, Round 4 — free climbing (no specific focus, just move). Rest 2 minutes between each set of four.

*One-move problem (5 minutes):* Identify a single move on a boulder problem that she finds challenging. Attempt it 8–10 times with full rest between attempts. This is deliberate practice on a specific skill — the most effective form of technique development.

**Week 10 — Volume and Pacing**

*Pyramid climbing (15 minutes):* Climb a pyramid of routes — 2 routes at a comfortable grade, 1 route one grade harder, 2 routes at the comfortable grade. Rest 3 minutes between routes. Focus on pacing — climbing at a speed that allows her to rest on the route and recover between hard moves. This directly mimics the demands of a long climbing day.

**Week 11 — Performance Climbing**

*Redpoint attempts (15 minutes):* Choose one or two routes or problems at or near her current limit. Make genuine redpoint attempts — full effort, full commitment, full rest between attempts (5 minutes minimum). This is the closest the Saturday session comes to actual performance climbing and is the most direct preparation for the Week 12 trip.

**Week 12 — Easy and Joyful**

15 minutes of easy, enjoyable climbing at well below her limit. No objectives, no performance pressure. This is the final session before the trip — the goal is to feel good, move well, and arrive at the trip psychologically fresh and excited.

### Block B — Strength Circuit (Phase 3)

**Phase 3 Circuit Structure:** 6 exercises, 4 rounds, 20 seconds rest between exercises, 2 minutes rest between rounds. This is the most demanding circuit of the programme — the short rest between exercises creates significant metabolic stress while the 2-minute round rest allows partial recovery.

**Week 9 Circuit:**

*1. Barbell Romanian Deadlift (8 reps, heavy):* Progress from the dumbbell version. The barbell allows heavier loading and develops the posterior chain strength needed for long days carrying a pack.

*2. Weighted Pull-Down (8 reps, heavy):* Neutral grip, same as the strength programme. Reinforce the primary climbing pulling pattern.

*3. Bulgarian Split Squat (8 reps each side, dumbbells):* Heavier than Phase 2. Add a 3-second eccentric.

*5. Hanging Knee Raise (12 reps):* From the pull-up bar, both hands, controlled. Lift the knees to 90° and lower slowly. This develops the hip flexor strength needed for high steps and the hanging shoulder stability needed for climbing. Monitor the right shoulder throughout.

**Week 11 Circuit:** Same loads as Week 10. Reduce to 3 rounds — this is the intensification week and volume is managed carefully. Increase the load on the landmine press by 5%.

## Master Reference Sheet

Before the week-by-week detail begins, every governing principle, every constraint, and every metric that runs across all 12 weeks is collected here. Read this section in full before implementing any session. It is the lens through which every programming decision in this document was made.

**The one rule that never changes:** If she reports pain above 0/10 in the right shoulder during any exercise, that exercise stops immediately. Not modified — stopped. Modify or replace it before the next session. Pain during a session is not a signal to push through. It is clinical information that requires a response.

**Physiotherapy communication:** Share this programme with her physiotherapist before Week 1 begins. Request a check-in at the end of Weeks 4, 8, and 12. This includes overhead press variations, pull-ups taken to full overhead range, behind-the-neck anything, and any exercise where the arm travels above 90° of elevation under load. ## The Daily Morning Mobility Routine
### Performed Every Morning, All 12 Weeks, Before Anything Else (8–10 minutes)

This routine never changes. Consistency across all 12 weeks is the mechanism of adaptation. The nervous system learns to trust these ranges through daily repetition, not through occasional intensive sessions.

**1. Thoracic Rotation in 90/90 (2 minutes)**
Lie on the right side, both hips and knees bent to 90°, pillow between the knees. Both arms extended in front at shoulder height. Keeping the hips completely still, rotate the top (left) arm open toward the ceiling and as far toward the floor on the other side as comfortable. Follow with the eyes and head. Hold the end position for 3 slow breaths — inhale 4 counts, exhale 6 counts. **3. Hip 90/90 with Forward Fold (2 minutes)**
Seated, both legs bent to 90° — one in front, one behind. Sit tall for 4 breaths. Hinge forward over the front leg for 4 breaths. Lean toward the back leg for 4 breaths. Switch sides.

**4. Doorway Pec Stretch at 90° (60 seconds each side)**
Forearm vertical on the door frame, elbow at 90°, upper arm parallel to the floor. Rotate the body away until a stretch is felt across the chest and anterior shoulder. Do not elevate the arm above 90°. 60 seconds each side with slow breathing.

**5. Neck and Upper Trapezius Release (90 seconds)**
Drop the right ear toward the right shoulder. Left hand rests gently on the left side of the head — no pulling. 4 breaths. Rotate the chin toward the right armpit. 4 breaths. Repeat on the other side.

**1. Sleeper Stretch (2 minutes right side, 90 seconds left)**
Lie on the right side, right arm extended at shoulder height, elbow bent to 90°, forearm pointing toward the ceiling. Use the left hand to gently press the right forearm toward the floor — internally rotating the right shoulder. Stop at any discomfort. Target sensation is a deep stretch in the posterior right shoulder. 4 repetitions of 20-second holds on the right, then switch.

**2. Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller (2 minutes)**
Foam roller perpendicular to the spine at the mid-back. Support the head with both hands. Extend over the roller, hold for 3 breaths, move one segment up the spine. Work from T12 to T4 — approximately 5–6 positions.

**3. Doorway Pec Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Same as morning routine.

**4. Cross-Body Posterior Capsule Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Right arm across the body at shoulder height. Left hand gently presses the right arm closer to the chest. 60 seconds with slow breathing.

**5. Wrist Flexor and Extensor Stretch (2 minutes)**
Right arm extended, palm up, left hand pulls fingers back — 30 seconds. Palm down, press fingers toward the body — 30 seconds. Repeat left side.

**6. Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Stretch (90 seconds each side)**
Half-kneeling, posterior pelvic tilt, shift hips forward until a stretch is felt in the front of the rear hip. 90 seconds each side.

**1. Standing Quad and Hip Flexor Stretch (90 seconds each side)**
Standing on one leg, pull the opposite foot toward the glutes. Tuck the pelvis under to increase the hip flexor component.

**2. Pigeon Pose or Supine Figure-Four (2 minutes each side)**
Pigeon on the floor or supine figure-four. 2 minutes each side with slow breathing.

**3. Calf and Achilles Stretch (60 seconds each side)**
Facing a wall, rear foot pressed into the floor. 30 seconds straight knee (gastrocnemius), 30 seconds bent knee (soleus and Achilles). Each side.

**4. Thoracic Rotation in 90/90 (90 seconds each side)**
Same as morning routine. Reinforce the morning work.

**5. Glute and Piriformis Foam Roll (2 minutes)**
Sit on the foam roller, one ankle crossed over the opposite knee. Roll slowly over the glute and piriformis. Pause on tender spots for 5–10 seconds. Switch sides.

**1. Forearm Flexor Stretch Sequence (3 minutes)**
Four positions, 45 seconds each: prayer stretch, reverse prayer, extended arm flexor stretch, extended arm extensor stretch.

**2. Finger Tendon Mobilisation (2 minutes)**
Loose fist to full finger extension, hold 3 seconds, repeat 10 times. Then individual finger circles — 5 each direction per finger.

**3. Sleeper Stretch (2 minutes right, 90 seconds left)**
Same as post-strength version.

**4. Thoracic Extension over Foam Roller (2 minutes)**
Same as post-strength version.

**5. Hip 90/90 with Rotation (2 minutes each side)**
Same as morning routine but held longer.

**6. Doorway Pec Stretch (90 seconds each side)**
Same as morning routine.

**7. Wrist Circles and Loaded Wrist Mobility (2 minutes)**
Large slow wrist circles, 10 each direction. Then palms flat on the floor, rock forward over the wrists into extension. Hold end position for 3 breaths.

### Performed After the Saturday Finisher Session, All 12 Weeks

**1. Thoracic Spine Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**
Foam roller thoracic extension — 3 minutes, spending longer at T4–T6. Thread the needle — on hands and knees, slide the right arm under the body along the floor, rotating until the right shoulder and ear rest on the floor, left arm reaching toward the ceiling. Hold for 4 slow breaths. 5 repetitions each side. Thoracic rotation in 90/90 — same as morning routine but 5 breaths at end range rather than 3. 3 minutes.

**2. Shoulder Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**
Sleeper stretch — 3 minutes right side, 2 minutes left. Shoulder CARs — pin the right shoulder blade against the rib cage with the left hand. Slowly rotate the right arm through the largest pain-free circle possible. 5 circles each direction. Doorway pec stretch with breathing — 90 seconds each side, using each exhale to allow the chest to open slightly further.

**3. Hip Comprehensive Sequence (8 minutes)**
Hip 90/90 with all variations — 60 seconds base position each side, 60 seconds forward fold each side, 60 seconds lateral lean each side. Deep squat hold — feet shoulder-width, toes turned out, lower into a deep squat, hold for 2 minutes. Use a doorframe for support if needed to keep heels down. Lateral lunge with hip shift and rotation — wide lateral step, shift hips back and to the side, rotate torso toward the bent knee at the bottom. 4 breaths. 6 repetitions each side.

**4. Wrist and Finger Comprehensive Sequence (4 minutes)**
Loaded wrist mobility in all directions — tabletop position, 30 seconds each direction. Finger tendon gliding exercises — straight fist, full fist, hook fist, tabletop position. 10 repetitions through the sequence.

## Sunday Recovery Mobility Session (20–25 minutes)
### All 12 Weeks

**1. Supine Breathing and Body Scan (3 minutes)**
Lying on the back, knees bent, one hand on chest, one on belly. Belly breathing — inhale 4 counts, exhale 6 counts. After 2 minutes, slow mental body scan from feet to head.

**2. Supine Hip and Lower Back Sequence (6 minutes)**
Knees-to-chest hug with gentle side-to-side rocking — 60 seconds. Supine figure-four — 2 minutes each side. Supine spinal twist — right knee to chest, guide across the body to the left, right arm extended out to the side — 60 seconds each side.

**3. Prone Shoulder and Thoracic Sequence (6 minutes)**
Prone Y-T-W-L sequence with no weight — Y position (thumbs up, arms at 45°, lift to hip height, hold 5 seconds), T position (arms straight out to sides, thumbs up, lift and hold 5 seconds), W position (elbows bent, upper arms out to sides, squeeze shoulder blades, hold 5 seconds), L position (elbows bent to 90°, upper arms out to sides, rotate forearms toward floor then ceiling). 5 repetitions of each. Prone thoracic extension — hands beside shoulders, press upper body up keeping hips on the floor, hold for 5 breaths.

**4. Standing Shoulder and Neck Sequence (5 minutes)**
Doorway pec stretch — 90 seconds each side. Upper trapezius release — same as morning routine but 6 breaths each position. Shoulder CARs — same as Saturday session, 5 circles each direction each arm.

**5. Closing Breathing (3 minutes)**
Return to supine breathing position. 3 minutes of slow diaphragmatic breathing. Exhale fully on each breath. This activates the parasympathetic nervous system and consolidates the recovery work of the session.

# PHASE 1: FOUNDATION AND SCAPULAR CONTROL
## Weeks 1–4

### Phase Goals
Establish pain-free movement patterns across all exercises. Activate inhibited scapular stabilisers — particularly the lower trapezius and serratus anterior. Build connective tissue tolerance for the loading that follows in Phases 2 and 3. Identify her true working range on every exercise and document it. Establish all daily habits — morning mobility, collagen protocol, nutrition targets, hydration, sleep. No exercise should produce pain above 0/10 during or after any session. Mild muscle fatigue is expected and appropriate. Any joint discomfort is not.

## WEEK 1

### Monday — Strength Session A

**Warm-up (10 minutes)**
5 minutes arm-bike building from Zone 1 to Zone 2 by minute 4. Then 2 rounds of: 10 scapular wall slides (arms at 90° goalpost position, sliding up only to comfortable range), 10 prone Y-raises with no weight (lying face down on a bench, arms at 45° from the body, thumbs up, lifting only to hip height), 10 band pull-aparts at chest height with a light resistance band.

**Main Work**
A1. Seated Cable Row (neutral grip, elbows close to body) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Light load allowing full scapular retraction and depression at end range. Cue: chest tall, shoulder blades back and down. Rest 90 seconds.

A3. Dumbbell Chest-Supported Row (prone on incline bench, neutral grip, elbows at 45°) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Slight pause at the top of each rep. Rest 90 seconds.

**Accessory Work**

B3. Dumbbell Bicep Curl (seated, neutral/supinated grip) — 2 sets × 15 reps. Light load, full elbow range.

Post-strength protocol as described above. 10–12 minutes.

**Modality:** Stair climber or incline treadmill walk
**Total duration:** 25 minutes

Post-cardio protocol as described above. 10 minutes.

Same as Monday.

A3. Single-Arm Dumbbell Row (bench-supported) — 3 sets × 12 reps each side. Elbow driving back and slightly out. Ensure the right shoulder does not hike or internally rotate under load. Rest 90 seconds.

**Accessory Work**

B2. Prone Lower Trap Raise (on incline bench, thumbs up, arms at 135° Y position) — 3 sets × 10 reps with no weight or 0.5–1 kg. Lift only to hip height.

B3. Tricep Pushdown (cable, rope attachment) — 2 sets × 15 reps. Elbows stay at the sides, arms stay below 90°.

**Post-Session Mobility**
Post-strength protocol. 10–12 minutes.

### Thursday — Cardio Session 2

**Modality:** Stationary bike (upright)
**Total duration:** 30 minutes

Zone 2 throughout (RPE 5–6). Cadence 80–90 RPM at a resistance that achieves Zone 2 without dropping below 70 RPM.

**Post-Session Mobility**
Post-cardio protocol. 10 minutes.

**Warm-up**
Same as Monday.

**Main Work**

A2. Incline Dumbbell Press (bench at 30–45°, neutral grip) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Keeps the shoulder below 90° of elevation. If any anterior shoulder discomfort arises, reduce the incline further or replace with a second floor press variation. Rest 90 seconds.

A3. TRX or Ring Row (body at roughly 45° to the floor) — 3 sets × 12 reps. Cue scapular retraction and depression at the top.

**Accessory Work**

B2. Scapular Depression Hold (on parallel bars or dip station, arms straight, no dip) — 3 sets × 10-second holds. Actively depress the scapulae — push the shoulders down away from the ears.

B3. Hammer Curl — 2 sets × 15 reps. Neutral grip, controlled tempo.

**Post-Session Mobility**
Post-strength protocol. 10–12 minutes.

Stair Climber Pyramid: Minute 1 Zone 1, Minute 2 Zone 2, Minute 3 Zone 3, Minute 4 Zone 2, Minute 5 Zone 1. Rest 2 minutes. Repeat once.

25–30 minutes as described above. Perform immediately after the finisher.
